title: A test is a claim about behaviour someone will rely on
description: Why a passing test suite and a working feature are not the same fact, and what turns a test from decoration into a claim someone can actually stake a decision on.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a test that makes a checkable claim from one that can't fail meaningfully
Name who relies on a green test suite and what they're trusting it to mean

contentSections.title: What a test actually claims

contentSections.body: A pull request lands with 40 tests, all generated in one prompt, all green. The reviewer skims them, sees the checkmark, approves. Three weeks later, on-call gets paged: the discount code that should cap at 20% off is stacking to 60%. There's a test for that function. It's green right now, on the broken code.

contentSections.scenario: The test in question is `expect(applyDiscount(cart, code)).toBeDefined()` — it checks that the function returns *something*, not what.
contentSections.question: Why is this test green on code that charges the wrong amount?

options.label: The test doesn't check what value comes back, only that a value comes back
The test was written before the bug was introduced
The test framework has a bug

feedback.shape: Right. `toBeDefined()` passes for a correct total, a wrong total, a negative total — anything except `undefined`. It was never in a position to notice the discount stacking wrong, because it never looked at the number.
feedback.timing: Order doesn't matter here — this test would be exactly as green today whether it was written before or after the stacking bug. It isn't watching the value at all.
feedback.framework: The framework is working exactly as designed. The assertion it's running just doesn't test the thing anyone cares about.

contentSections.concept: A test is a claim: *if this behaviour were wrong, this test would fail.* `toBeDefined()` makes almost no claim — it can't distinguish correct output from most kinds of wrong output. The green checkmark on it is true and also tells nobody anything.

contentSections.body: This is the gap that matters: **a passing test suite and a working feature are different facts**, and the size of the gap between them is set entirely by what the tests actually assert. A suite can be 100% green and 30% meaningful. Nobody sees that difference on the PR page — the checkmark looks the same either way. Which means the only place the difference is visible is in the test code itself, at the moment someone decides what to assert.

contentSections.question: Before the next pod: what's the one question that tells you whether a test is a real claim, in a sentence you could ask about any test you're looking at right now?
contentSections.answer: Would this test fail if the code did the wrong thing it's supposed to be checking for?
contentSections.hint: Not "does it run" or "does it pass" — those are true of `toBeDefined()` too.

contentSections.body: A test that can't fail on a real bug isn't a weaker test — it isn't a test, whatever the checkmark says.

contentSections.title: Who's actually relying on that claim

contentSections.body: The reviewer who approved the PR isn't the only one trusting that green checkmark. Six months from now, someone refactors the discount module and runs the suite to see if they broke anything. The on-call engineer at 3am pulls up the test file to understand what the function is supposed to do. All three are reading the same green checkmark as the same claim — and if the claim is thin, all three get the same wrong confidence.

contentSections.scenario: A `sendInvoiceEmail(order)` function has one test: it calls the function and asserts no exception was thrown. Six months later someone changes the email template and accidentally drops the invoice total from the body. The test is still green. A customer emails support asking why their invoice shows no amount.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that let this ship?

options.label: The test asserts absence of a crash, not presence of the correct content
The person who changed the template didn't run the tests
Email templates can't be unit tested

feedback.absence: Exactly. "Didn't throw" and "contains the invoice total" are unrelated claims. A template with the total silently deleted still renders, still sends, still doesn't throw. The test was never watching for that.
feedback.didnt-run: They very likely did run it — and it passed, which is the actual problem. The test running isn't in question; what it was checking for is.
feedback.cant-test: They can — asserting the rendered email body contains the expected total is a normal, cheap string assertion. Nobody wrote it, which is different from it being untestable.

contentSections.mechanism: "No exception" and "correct behaviour" are almost unrelated claims for most bugs. Silently wrong output — a dropped field, a wrong total, a missing line — usually doesn't throw anything. A test suite full of not-crashed assertions gives everyone downstream (reviewer, future refactorer, on-call) false confidence about exactly the class of bug that's most common and least visible: the one that runs fine and does the wrong thing.

contentSections.body: This is why "a test is a claim" matters more than it sounds like it should: every person downstream of the suite — the reviewer approving the PR, the teammate refactoring later, the on-call engineer three weeks from now with no memory of this code — reads the same green checkmark and makes a decision based on it. None of them re-derive what the tests actually check. They trust the summary. Which means writing a test that doesn't check the real behaviour isn't a shortcut that saves time now; it's a debt that gets paid by whoever trusts the checkmark next, usually with less context than you have right now.

contentSections.scenario: A teammate is about to merge a PR with these four tests for a `refundOrder(orderId, amount)` function.
contentSections.question: Which of these are claims a future reader could actually rely on? Select all that apply.

items.label: expect(refundOrder(1, 20)).not.toBeNull()
expect(refundOrder(1, 20)).toEqual({ orderId: 1, refunded: 20, status: 'REFUNDED' })
expect(() => refundOrder(1, -5)).toThrow('Refund amount must be positive')
// TODO: test refund exceeding order total

explanation.a: Same shape as `toBeDefined()` — any non-null return, right or wrong, passes.
explanation.b: This commits to an exact expected object. If the function returns the wrong status, wrong amount, or wrong order id, this fails. That's a real claim.
explanation.c: This commits to a specific error and a specific triggering input. A future reader can trust that negative amounts are rejected, because if that behaviour broke, this test would catch it.
explanation.d: A comment isn't a test — it can't fail, so it can't be relied on for anything. It's a note to a human, not a claim the suite makes.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of these four are real claims. The other two look like coverage in a PR diff and add nothing to what anyone could actually trust — which is worth noticing, because from the outside (a PR review, a file listing), all four look identical: four lines under `describe('refundOrder')`.

contentSections.body: Every person who trusts a green checkmark — reviewer, future teammate, on-call — is trusting the specific claims inside it, whether or not they ever read them.

title: Specifying tests instead of asking for "some tests"
description: Turning a vague request for tests into a specification an AI assistant — or a teammate — can't misread, by naming the cases and the expected outcome for each before asking for code.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a vague test request into a list of named cases with expected outcomes
Recognise which parts of a test request are being left to the assistant to invent

contentSections.title: What "write some tests" actually delegates

contentSections.body: "Write tests for `applyDiscountCode`" produces 12 tests in four seconds. All plausible-looking, all green. Nobody chose which cases matter — the assistant did, quietly, by picking whatever came to mind first. That's the same as asking a contractor to "build a good deck" and being surprised it's not the deck you needed.

contentSections.scenario: A request goes out: "Write unit tests for the login rate limiter." The assistant returns tests for: three failed attempts allowed, a fourth attempt blocked, and a successful login resetting the counter.
contentSections.question: What's missing that the request never ruled in or out?

options.label: Whether the block expires, and after how long
Nothing — three cases is already thorough
The test file's naming convention

feedback.expiry: Right — and it's not a nitpick. A rate limiter that blocks forever versus one that unblocks after 15 minutes are two completely different features, and "write tests for the login rate limiter" specified neither. The assistant picked the three cases that occurred to it and moved on; a lockout-expiry case wasn't in that set, so nobody decided whether it matters.
feedback.nothing: Three cases sounds thorough until you ask what happens after the block — does it ever lift? The request never said, so the assistant never tested it, so nobody knows what the code actually does there.
feedback.naming: File naming is a real thing to care about, but it's not the gap that matters here — the gap is a whole behaviour (block expiry) that was never specified as in-scope or out.

contentSections.concept: A vague request doesn't produce fewer tests — it produces tests for whichever cases were easiest to think of, with no signal about which cases were considered and rejected versus never considered at all. Specifying is naming the cases yourself, before asking for code, so the gap between "cases I thought about" and "cases the suite covers" is a choice instead of an accident.

contentSections.body: The fix isn't writing more tests, and it isn't writing longer prompts either — it's naming the *cases*, not the topic. "Test the rate limiter" names a topic. "Test: three failed attempts allowed, the fourth blocked, the block still active on attempt five, the block lifting after the cooldown window, and a successful login resetting the counter to zero" names cases. The second one can't be satisfied by three plausible-looking tests that all miss the actual question you needed answered — expiry.

contentSections.problem: You need tests for `canEditPost(user, post)`, which should return true if the user is the post's author, or the user has an `admin` role, and false otherwise — including when the post is soft-deleted, which nobody but an admin can edit. Specify the request.

steps.label: List the roles that matter
steps.work: Author (owns the post), admin, and "neither" — a logged-in user who is neither the author nor an admin.
steps.why: These are the three permission states the function branches on. Naming them is naming the cases, not the topic.

steps.label: Add the state that changes the rule
steps.work: Soft-deleted posts flip the rule: even the author loses edit access once deleted, only admin keeps it.
steps.why: This is the case a topic-level request ("test canEditPost") is least likely to surface, because it requires reading the spec closely rather than guessing from the function name.

steps.label: Name the expected outcome for each combination
steps.work: Author + not deleted → true. Author + deleted → false. Admin + deleted → true. Neither + not deleted → false.
steps.why: Naming the case without the expected outcome still leaves the assistant to guess what "correct" means — which is exactly the gap a specified request closes.

steps.label: Write the actual request
steps.work: "Write unit tests for canEditPost(user, post) covering: author editing their own non-deleted post (true), author trying to edit their own deleted post (false), admin editing any post regardless of deletion (true), and a non-author non-admin user (false)."
steps.why: Four named cases, four named outcomes. There's no case left for the assistant to invent, and no ambiguity about what counts as passing.

faded.problem: Now specify a request for `canCancelSubscription(user, subscription)`: only the subscription's owner can cancel it, and only if it hasn't already been cancelled — cancelling a subscription that's already cancelled should return an error rather than silently succeeding.

blanks.prompt: Name the two states of the subscription that change the outcome (two words each)
blanks.why: These are the two states the second rule branches on — same move as naming author/admin/neither in the worked example.

blanks.prompt: For the owner cancelling an already-cancelled subscription, what should the outcome be? (one short phrase)
blanks.why: This is the case most likely to get silently skipped by a vague request — "cancel a subscription" reads as one happy path, not two states with different required outcomes.

blanks.prompt: Besides the owner, who else needs a named case? (one or two words)
blanks.why: Same shape as the admin/neither split — you need a case for someone who isn't allowed, not just cases for someone who is.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the states that change the outcome → name the outcome for each → write the request as that list, not as the function's name.** A request that names states and outcomes leaves nothing for the assistant to invent; a request that names only the function leaves everything to it.

contentSections.body: Naming cases and expected outcomes before you ask is the entire difference between commissioning tests and hoping for them.

contentSections.title: Reading what got left to guesswork

contentSections.body: Sometimes the request is already written and you're the one reading it — reviewing a teammate's prompt, or your own from two days ago. Spotting what was left vague is a skill on its own, separate from writing a specified one.

contentSections.intro: You're specifying a request for tests on `calculateLoyaltyPoints(purchaseAmount, tier)`, where points are 1 per dollar for standard tier, 1.5 per dollar for gold tier, and purchases under $5 earn zero points regardless of tier. Build the request field by field.

fields.question: Which tiers need their own case?
options: Just gold, since it's the special one
Standard and gold, since the rate differs between them
Every possible tier name that might exist in the system
fields.correctValue: Standard and gold, since the rate differs between them
fields.feedback: You need a case for each rate the function actually branches on — testing only gold leaves the standard-tier math completely unverified.

fields.question: How should the $5 minimum be specified?
options: "A $4.99 purchase earns 0 points regardless of tier; a $5.00 purchase earns points normally"
fields.correctValue: "A $4.99 purchase earns 0 points regardless of tier; a $5.00 purchase earns points normally"
fields.feedback: "Fewer points" and "edge cases" both leave the actual threshold value and the exact expected outcome to be guessed. Naming $4.99 and $5.00 with their outcomes removes the guesswork — including the boundary itself, which off-by-one bugs live on.

fields.question: A $10 gold purchase earns 15 points exactly, but a $7 gold purchase earns 10.5 — should the request say anything about this?
options: No, rounding is an implementation detail the assistant can decide
Yes — name whether 10.5 should round, truncate, or stay fractional, and to what
No, non-integer cases are too rare to bother with
fields.correctValue: Yes — name whether 10.5 should round, truncate, or stay fractional, and to what
fields.feedback: This is exactly the kind of decision that's easy to leave unspecified and expensive to leave unspecified — whichever way the assistant guesses becomes the de facto behaviour, discovered later by whoever notices their point balance doesn't match their receipt.

contentSections.synthesis: A specified request for this function names: the standard-tier case, the gold-tier case, the $4.99-vs-$5.00 boundary with both outcomes, and an explicit rounding rule. That's four decisions that a topic-level request ("test calculateLoyaltyPoints") would have silently delegated to whichever plausible guess came first.

contentSections.body: A useful habit for reading a request someone else wrote: look for the sentence that isn't there. "Test the checkout flow" has no sentence about partial stock, no sentence about a payment that times out mid-request, no sentence about a cart that expires while the user is on the payment page. None of those are exotic — they're the actual failure modes of a real checkout — and none of them are ruled in or out by "test the checkout flow." The assistant will pick something. What it picks is not a decision anyone made on purpose.
The gap between a vague request and a specified one is never about effort — it's about which decisions you made on purpose and which ones you let happen by default.

title: The cases a generated suite always misses
description: Why a suite generated by reading the implementation tests what the code does instead of what it was supposed to handle — and the specific families of case that fall into that gap.

learningObjectives.text: Identify why generated suites systematically mirror the implementation's happy path
Name the recurring categories of case a generated suite tends to miss

contentSections.title: Why the gap is systematic, not random

contentSections.body: Ask an assistant to write tests for a function by showing it the function. It reads the code, and the code only does what it was written to do — so the tests it writes exercise exactly that. This isn't a quality problem with any particular model. It's a structural one: you can't derive "what should happen on malformed input" by reading code that never considered malformed input.

contentSections.scenario: A function `getDiscountForZone(zone)` has an if/else chain for 'north', 'south', 'east', 'west', returning 0 for anything else via a final `else`. An assistant is shown this function and asked to write tests.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely gap in the resulting suite?

options.label: A test for zone = null or an empty string, since neither is a named branch
A test for zone = 'north', since that's the first branch
Nothing — the else clause means every input is handled

feedback.null-zone: Right. The else clause does technically handle null — it returns 0 — but whether that's *correct* behaviour (should an unrecognised zone silently get no discount, or should it be an error that surfaces a data problem?) is a product decision nobody made. The generated suite will very likely test the four named zones and skip this, because null was never a branch the code drew attention to.
feedback.north: That's almost certainly covered — it's the most obvious case, the first branch, the one a model reading the code would generate a test for without any extra thought.
feedback.handled: The code *runs* without throwing on any input, which is different from the behaviour being correct or intended. "Doesn't crash" and "does the right thing" are the two claims that get conflated here.

contentSections.concept: A generated suite mirrors the implementation's own structure: one test per branch, roughly. Branches the code doesn't have — invalid input, concurrent calls, empty collections, the zero case, the case where two things happen at once — don't get a test, because there was no branch to prompt one. The suite ends up matching the code's *shape*, not the domain's actual range of possible input.

contentSections.body: There's a name worth having for this: **generated tests test what the code does, not what the code was supposed to do.** The two overlap heavily for correct code and diverge exactly where it matters most — where the implementation itself has a gap, the tests derived from reading that implementation inherit the same blind spot. A suite with 100% branch coverage of a buggy function proves the tests match the bug, not that the bug isn't there.

contentSections.question: Name one category of input that's almost never in a generated suite unless someone explicitly asks for it, and that has nothing to do with the number of branches in the code.
contentSections.answer: Concurrent or out-of-order calls — e.g. two requests to cancel the same order arriving at nearly the same time. Nothing in a single function's source code hints that it might be called twice at once, so a suite built from reading the function alone essentially never covers it.
contentSections.hint: Think about what happens when the same operation runs twice, at the same time, on the same data.

contentSections.body: A suite generated by reading the implementation inherits exactly the implementation's blind spots — which is the worst possible correlation for a test suite to have.

contentSections.title: The recurring families worth checking for by hand

contentSections.body: Not every missing case is exotic. A small, repeatable list catches most of what a generated suite drops — worth running through deliberately rather than trusting that "write thorough tests" will surface them.

contentSections.scenario: A generated suite exists for `mergeCartItems(cartA, cartB)`, which combines two shopping carts into one, summing quantities for items that appear in both.
contentSections.question: Which of these cases is the suite likely to be missing, based on what a generated suite typically skips?

items.label: Both carts have several different items, none overlapping
One of the two carts is completely empty
Both carts contain the same item, quantities should sum
Combined quantity for one item would exceed the maximum the system allows per line
One cart has the same item listed on two separate lines (a pre-existing data bug), both need merging correctly

explanation.both-populated: This is the obvious happy path and is almost certainly already covered — it's the first thing anyone, human or model, thinks of.
explanation.one-empty: An empty cart isn't a 'normal' input in the sense the function's core logic was written around, so it's a classic omission — does merging with empty return the other cart unchanged, or throw, or return empty?
explanation.same-item-overlap: This is the function's whole reason for existing (summing quantities), so it's near-certainly tested already.
explanation.quantity-overflow: This requires knowing there's a business rule (a max per line) that lives outside the merge function itself — a generated suite reading only this function has no way to know that rule exists.
explanation.duplicate-lines: This requires imagining messy real-world data the function's own logic doesn't anticipate. Nothing in the function signature hints that a cart could already be malformed coming in.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the misses: empty/zero input, limits and boundaries defined *elsewhere* in the system, and malformed input that the function assumes won't happen. None of these are visible from reading the function in isolation — which is exactly why a suite generated that way misses them reliably, not occasionally.

contentSections.body: Four families worth checking for by hand, every time: **empty or zero input** (empty list, zero quantity, blank string), **limits defined elsewhere** (a max the function itself doesn't enforce or even know about), **malformed or already-inconsistent input** (data that shouldn't exist but sometimes does), and **concurrent or repeated calls** (the same action happening twice). None require being an expert in the domain — they require asking "what if this input weren't the tidy kind the function was written assuming?" before accepting the suite as done.
A generated suite is a start, not a finish — check it against empty input, outside limits, malformed data, and repeated calls before trusting it's thorough.

title: Mutation thinking: would this test notice?
description: A concrete way to check whether a passing test is actually watching for the bug it claims to catch — break the code on purpose and see if anything notices.

learningObjectives.text: Apply mutation thinking to judge whether an existing test would catch a specific class of bug
Identify which mutation a given test is and isn't sensitive to

contentSections.title: Breaking the code on purpose

contentSections.body: A test suite passes. That's one fact. Whether the suite would have caught the last three bugs your team actually shipped is a completely different fact, and "it passes" tells you nothing about it. Mutation thinking is the cheap way to close that gap without waiting for the next real bug to teach you.

contentSections.scenario: A team runs a mutation-testing tool against a module with 85% line coverage — meaning 85% of the code's lines execute during the test run.
contentSections.question: Roughly what percentage of small, deliberate bugs introduced into that module (off-by-one changes, flipped comparisons, swapped operators) do you think the existing tests actually catch?
contentSections.explanation: Coverage measures whether a line ran during the tests, not whether any assertion depended on that line doing the right thing. It's common for well-covered code to have a much lower mutation-kill rate than its coverage number suggests, because plenty of "covered" lines are executed by a test that's asserting something else entirely — the test walks through the code without ever checking the specific value that line produces. High coverage with a low kill rate is one of the more common and more misleading gaps in a codebase that looks well-tested from the coverage number alone.

contentSections.body: Mutation thinking is the manual version of what that tool automates: **pick one small, specific way the code could be wrong, change the code to be wrong that way, and run the suite.** If nothing fails, you've found a test that wasn't actually watching for that bug — regardless of how green it looked a minute ago. It's a few minutes of deliberate effort per function, and it answers a question coverage numbers can't: not "did the tests run this line" but "would the tests have caught it if this line were wrong."

contentSections.problem: A function `isWithinBusinessHours(hour)` returns true for `hour >= 9 && hour < 17`. The one existing test asserts `isWithinBusinessHours(12)` is true. Apply mutation thinking: is the suite adequate?

steps.label: Pick a small mutation
steps.work: Change `hour < 17` to `hour <= 17`, so 5pm now counts as within business hours.
steps.why: A single-character mutation on a boundary comparison is one of the most common real bugs — this is exactly the shape a typo or a hasty edit produces.

steps.label: Run the existing test against the mutant
steps.work: isWithinBusinessHours(12) is true under both the original and the mutant — 12 is nowhere near either version of the boundary.
steps.why: The test's only input, 12, sits comfortably inside the range under both versions of the code, so it can't distinguish them.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.work: The suite does not catch this mutation. It passes on both the correct code and the subtly wrong code.
steps.why: This is the actual finding mutation thinking produces — not a vague sense that more tests would be nice, but a specific, named gap: the boundary at 17 is unverified.

steps.label: Write the test that would catch it
steps.work: Add: isWithinBusinessHours(17) should be false (17:00 is closing time, not open), and isWithinBusinessHours(16) should be true.
steps.why: These two values sit exactly where the original and the mutant disagree, which is the only place a test can distinguish them.

faded.problem: A function `canRentCar(driverAge)` returns true for `driverAge >= 25`. The one existing test asserts `canRentCar(30)` is true. A mutation changes the check to `driverAge > 25`.

blanks.prompt: Does the existing test (driverAge = 30) distinguish the original from the mutant? (yes or no)
blanks.why: 30 satisfies both `>= 25` and `> 25` identically — the test can't tell them apart.

blanks.prompt: What exact age value sits on the boundary where the two versions disagree?
blanks.why: At 25, the original says true (25 >= 25) and the mutant says false (25 is not > 25) — this is the only value where they diverge.

blanks.prompt: What should the new test assert for that value? (true or false)
blanks.why: The correct rule allows a 25-year-old to rent; asserting this value catches the mutation and confirms the intended boundary.

contentSections.procedure: **Pick a mutation → check whether any existing test uses an input where the mutation changes the outcome → if none does, write one that sits exactly on the boundary where they disagree.** Boundaries are where off-by-one mutations hide, which is why they're the first place to check.

contentSections.body: A test with no case sitting on a boundary can't tell a correct boundary from a wrong one, no matter how many other tests are green.

contentSections.title: Where to spend the effort

contentSections.body: Mutation thinking doesn't need to be run on every line of every function — that's slow and mostly redundant. It earns its keep fastest on the code where a subtle wrong answer is expensive and easy to miss by eye: money, permissions, and anything with a comparison operator.

contentSections.question: Mutating `daysSincePurchase > 30` to `daysSincePurchase >= 30` (so exactly 30 days becomes ineligible) — does the existing test catch this?

options.label: No — the test uses day 10, nowhere near the boundary at 30
Yes — the test explicitly checks the refund window
Can't tell without running it

feedback.no-catch: Right. Day 10 returns true under both `> 30` and `>= 30` — they only disagree at exactly day 30. This test checks that the window exists in some form, but not where its edge actually is.
feedback.yes-catch: It checks the *concept* of a refund window, but not the specific boundary value — those are different claims, and only a test using day 30 itself would distinguish `>` from `>=`.
feedback.unclear: It's fully determinable from the values involved — day 10 is nowhere near 30 under either version of the comparison, so the outcome is identical either way.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This function has exactly one boundary (day 30) and the suite has exactly zero tests near it. The fix is one line: `expect(isEligibleForRefund(30, 'good')).toBe(true)` — asserting that day 30 itself is still within the window, which is the value where a `>` vs `>=` typo would actually show up. Notice this isn't about writing *more* tests in general; it's about writing the one test that sits where the bug would actually hide.

contentSections.body: A rough prioritisation, since nobody has time to mutate everything: spend the effort on **comparisons involving money or a limit** (off-by-one on a threshold is cheap to make and expensive to ship), **permission and eligibility checks** (a flipped condition here is a security or billing bug, not a cosmetic one), and **anything where the existing test suite has exactly one case per function** — one test per function is the strongest signal that boundaries were never considered, because there was no second case to put on one.
Mutation thinking isn't a tool to run on everything — it's a five-minute check to run on the boundary that would be expensive to get wrong.

title: Fast, deterministic, and independent — or nobody runs them
description: The three properties that decide whether a test suite stays part of the workflow or quietly turns into a thing people route around — and what breaks each one.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the mechanism by which slow, flaky, or coupled tests stop being trusted or run
Diagnose which of the three properties a given test smell violates

contentSections.title: The three properties, and what breaks them

contentSections.body: A test suite that's correct in principle but takes 40 minutes and fails randomly 1 time in 20 is not, in practice, a test suite anyone relies on. It's a suite people re-run, then skip, then eventually stop noticing. Correctness on paper and correctness in practice diverge here in a very specific, very common way.

contentSections.scenario: A test for `sendPasswordResetEmail(email)` calls the real production email provider's API every time it runs, and asserts the API responded with success.
contentSections.question: What property does this test violate, and what actually goes wrong as a result?

options.label: Determinism — a transient provider timeout fails the test with nothing wrong in the code
Independence — it depends on another test's leftover state
Nothing — testing the real integration is the whole point

feedback.determinism: Right. Every run now depends on the email provider's uptime, rate limits, and network latency — none of which are properties of your code. A transient timeout on the provider's end fails this test even when nothing about the code changed.
feedback.independence: Independence is about tests depending on each other's state, which isn't what's happening here — this test could run completely alone and still fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the code.
feedback.nothing: Testing the real integration has value, but not as a test that runs on every commit — that's what a small number of clearly-separated integration tests are for, not the main unit suite.

contentSections.concept: **Deterministic** means the test's outcome depends only on the code, not on the network, the clock, or which tests ran before it. **Fast** means it doesn't cost enough time that people start skipping it. **Independent** means it doesn't need another test's leftover state to make sense. Break any one, and the suite still runs — it just stops being something anyone can trust the result of, which in practice is the same as not having it.

contentSections.body: Each property fails a different way, and it's worth knowing which one you're looking at, because the fixes are different. **Non-determinism** — a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change — usually traces to the real clock, real network calls, or unseeded randomness. **Slowness** traces to real I/O the test doesn't need: hitting an actual database or file system when an in-memory fake would do. **Coupling** traces to shared state — a global variable, a shared database row, a fixture object — that one test mutates and another reads, so the result depends on run order.

contentSections.question: A test suite has one test that fails about once every 30 runs, for no code-related reason. What's the realistic long-run cost of leaving it as-is, beyond the occasional annoying re-run?
contentSections.answer: People learn the pattern — "that one's just flaky" — and start re-running red builds without reading them closely. Once that habit sets in, a real failure that happens to land on the same test (or looks similar) gets waved through the same way, which is the actual cost: not the 1-in-30 itself, but what it trains people to do with every red build afterward.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a person does the third time a red build turns out to be nothing.

contentSections.body: A test that's occasionally wrong for reasons unrelated to the code is worse than no test — it trains people to stop trusting red.

contentSections.title: Fixing each one without losing the coverage

contentSections.body: None of these three problems requires deleting the test and losing what it checks. Each has a standard fix that keeps the claim while removing what made it slow, flaky, or coupled.

contentSections.question: A test hits a real Postgres database, takes 800ms, and occasionally fails when the CI database is under load from other jobs. Put these fix steps in the order you'd actually do them.
steps: Identify exactly what the test needs from the database — which rows, which query results
Replace the real database with an in-memory fake or a mocked query layer that returns those exact results
Rerun the test and confirm it still fails when the code is deliberately broken
Move any test that genuinely needs to verify real database behaviour into a small, separately-run integration suite
contentSections.explanation: You can't fake what you haven't named, so identifying the exact data the test needs comes first. Swapping in a fake without checking it can still fail (step 3) risks ending up with a test that always passes regardless of the code — determinism traded for a test that can't fail at all, which is worse. And not every database-touching test should become a fake; some genuinely need to verify the real thing, which is what a small, clearly-labelled integration suite is for.

contentSections.body: The independence fix is usually the cheapest of the three and the most often skipped: give every test its own setup and its own teardown, so it never depends on what another test left behind. This sometimes feels like duplication — three tests each creating their own user record instead of sharing one — but that duplication is what buys the property that a test's result doesn't depend on which other tests happened to run first, or whether someone re-ran just this one file in isolation.
Fast, deterministic and independent aren't extra credit — they're what keeps a correct test suite from turning into one nobody actually runs.

title: Practice — Strengthen Eight Weak Tests So They Can Fail
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: take a test that's currently unable to catch the bug it claims to guard against, and fix it. This is where mutation thinking and specification stop being things you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply mutation thinking and specification to strengthen weak tests at speed

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Same skills as the five lessons, applied to eight fresh cases. Do them in one sitting or spread across the day — nothing here is timed or expires.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for on the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Commission and Harden a Suite for an Untested Module
description: Take a described, currently-untested module, specify and commission its test suite, then prove every test in it can actually fail by mutating the implementation and confirming the suite notices.

learningObjectives.text: Specify a complete test request for an untested module before generating any code
Prove a generated test suite's claims by deliberately breaking the implementation it tests

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the module's real assessment: not writing tests, but commissioning a suite you can prove is trustworthy — with the receipts to show it, not just a green run.

contentSections.title: Harden a suite for an untested module
contentSections.brief: You've inherited `applyBulkDiscount(items, discountPercent, maxDiscountAmount)` — a function used at checkout that applies a percentage discount across a cart's items, capped at a maximum dollar amount, with no existing tests. Before it ships to production, it needs a suite you can stand behind — not one that merely exists.
contentSections.deliverable: A suite where every test has been shown to fail against a deliberately broken version of the function — with a short log, for each test, of the mutation it caught.

stages.title: Specify the cases before generating anything
stages.instructions: Write out the case list first, in plain language, before asking an assistant for a single line of test code. Include: the normal case (discount applies cleanly, under the cap), the cap actually binding (discount would exceed maxDiscountAmount, so it's clamped), an empty items list, a discountPercent of 0, and a discountPercent of 100. For each, state the expected numeric outcome — not just the scenario name.
stages.checkpoint: You have five named cases, each with a specific expected number or behaviour written down, not just a description of the scenario.

stages.title: Commission the suite against that spec
stages.instructions: Turn your case list into the actual request you'd send an assistant (or write the tests directly, if you prefer) — one test per case, each asserting the exact expected value from stage 1. Every assertion should commit to a specific number, not a type check or a not-null check.
stages.checkpoint: You have five tests, each asserting a specific expected value, matching the cases from stage 1 one-to-one.

stages.title: Mutate the implementation and check the suite notices
stages.instructions: Write (or describe precisely enough to reason through) four separate one-line mutations to the function: flip the cap comparison from `>` to `>=`, change the discount math to apply before rather than after the cap check, change the empty-list handling to return `null` instead of an empty result, and change 100% discount to leave a $0.01 residual instead of exactly zero. For each mutation, determine whether your suite from stage 2 would catch it.
stages.checkpoint: For each of the four mutations, you have a clear yes/no on whether an existing test catches it, with the specific test named if yes.

stages.title: Harden any test that didn't catch its mutation
stages.instructions: For every mutation stage 3 found uncaught, write the additional test that would catch it — sitting exactly on the boundary or case the mutation affects, the way lesson four's worked examples did. Confirm (by reasoning through the values, since you may not have a runnable environment) that the new test fails against the mutant and passes against the original.
stages.checkpoint: Every one of the four mutations from stage 3 now has a specific test that would catch it, and you can state which test and why.

rubric.criterion: Cases were specified before code was requested
rubric.meets: The stage-1 case list exists as written text with expected outcomes, not reconstructed after the fact from whatever tests got generated.

rubric.criterion: Every assertion commits to a specific value
rubric.meets: No test in the suite uses a not-null, type, or 'doesn't throw' check where an exact expected value was available.

rubric.criterion: All four mutations were actually checked, not assumed
rubric.meets: Each of the four mutations has an explicit yes/no with reasoning, not a general sense that 'the tests probably cover it.'

rubric.criterion: Every uncaught mutation got a real fix
rubric.meets: Each gap from stage 3 has a specific new test, sitting on the exact value where the mutation and the original disagree — not a vaguely 'more thorough' test.

rubric.criterion: The deliverable is legible to someone else
rubric.meets: A teammate could read the mutation log and understand, for each test, what specific bug it would catch and why — without re-deriving your reasoning.

contentSections.body: A suite you've proven catches specific bugs is a different, stronger thing than a suite that merely runs — and now you have the log to show which is which.

title: Checkpoint — Tests You Can Trust
description: Ten questions pulling from this module. Ungraded, untimed — anything that doesn't come back now returns in a later checkpoint.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Tests You Can Trust

questions.from: This module — A test is a claim about behaviour someone will rely on
questions.prompt: What makes a test a claim someone can rely on, rather than decoration?

options.label: It asserts a specific expected outcome that would change if the code were wrong
It's written in a describe/it block with a clear name
It runs quickly as part of CI

questions.explanation: A clear name and a fast runtime are nice properties, but neither makes the test able to fail on a real bug. Only a specific, checkable assertion does that.

questions.from: This module — Specifying tests instead of asking for "some tests"
questions.prompt: What's the key difference between "test the rate limiter" and a specified request?

options.label: The specified request names the cases and the expected outcome for each
The specified request is always longer
The specified request avoids using an AI assistant entirely

questions.explanation: Length isn't the point, and specification works fine alongside an assistant — the point is naming which cases matter and what correct looks like for each, so nothing is left for the assistant to guess.

questions.from: This module — The cases a generated suite always misses
questions.prompt: Why does a suite generated by reading an implementation tend to miss malformed or empty input?

options.label: The implementation itself gives no hint that such input might occur
Models are bad at writing tests for edge cases in general
Malformed input is too rare to matter

questions.explanation: A suite derived from reading code inherits that code's own blind spots — if the implementation never considered an input, nothing in it prompts a test for that input either. This isn't a model-quality issue, it's structural.

questions.from: This module — The cases a generated suite always misses
questions.prompt: Which of these is a business rule a generated suite is least likely to catch, because it lives outside the function being tested?

options.label: A maximum quantity per line, enforced by a different part of the system
The function's main happy-path calculation
A named branch that already exists in the if/else chain

questions.explanation: A limit defined elsewhere in the system is invisible to a suite generated purely by reading the one function in isolation — there's nothing in that function's code hinting the limit exists.

questions.from: This module — Mutation thinking: would this test notice?
questions.prompt: What does mutation thinking actually check, that code coverage doesn't?

options.label: Whether a test would fail if the code were deliberately made wrong
How many lines of code execute during the test run
How fast the test suite runs

questions.explanation: Coverage measures whether a line ran; mutation thinking measures whether anything would notice if that line's logic were wrong. High coverage with a low mutation-catch rate is common and easy to miss.

questions.from: This module — Mutation thinking: would this test notice?
questions.prompt: A test uses input 30 for a rule with boundary `days > 30`. What's the fastest way to find out if it catches an off-by-one mutation to `>=`?

options.label: Check whether the test's input value sits exactly on the boundary where the two versions disagree
Read the test's name and see if it mentions the boundary
Assume it's fine if the test is currently passing

questions.explanation: A passing test tells you nothing about whether it would catch a specific mutation — only checking whether the input sits where the two versions actually disagree tells you that.

questions.from: This module — Fast, deterministic, and independent — or nobody runs them
questions.prompt: A test hits a real third-party API and occasionally fails when that API is slow. Which property does this violate?

options.label: Determinism — the outcome now depends on something other than the code
Independence — it depends on another test's state
Nothing, as long as it usually passes

questions.explanation: The test's result now depends on the third party's uptime and latency, not on whether the code is correct — that's the definition of a non-deterministic test.

questions.from: This module — Fast, deterministic, and independent — or nobody runs them
questions.prompt: What's the realistic long-run effect of a test that fails for unrelated reasons about 1 time in 20?

options.label: People learn to distrust red builds and start re-running or ignoring failures
It has no effect as long as it's rare
The team immediately rewrites the whole suite

questions.explanation: The real cost of a flaky test isn't the occasional false failure — it's what that trains people to do the next time any test fails, including a real one.

questions.from: This module — A test is a claim about behaviour someone will rely on
questions.prompt: Who, besides the person who wrote a test, ends up relying on what it actually checks?

options.label: The reviewer approving the PR, a future teammate refactoring the code, and on-call responding to an incident
Nobody — tests are only read by the author
Only the CI system

questions.explanation: Everyone downstream reads the same green checkmark as the same claim, usually without re-deriving what it actually checks — which is why a thin test's cost is paid by someone with less context than the author had.

questions.from: This module — Specifying tests instead of asking for "some tests"
questions.prompt: A specified test request leaves nothing for the assistant to do except what?

options.label: Turn the named cases and expected outcomes into working test code
Decide which cases matter
Decide what correct behaviour looks like

questions.explanation: Once the cases and expected outcomes are named, the only remaining job is translating that into runnable code — the two decisions that actually matter (which cases, what's correct) were made by the person specifying, not left to the assistant.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back today returns in a later checkpoint — that's the design, not a gap.

title: The pull request description as the reviewer's only context
description: Why the description is not a formality but the entire interface between what you know and what a cold reviewer knows — and what it needs to contain to actually work.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what information a cold reviewer lacks that only the author can supply
Write a PR description that lets a reviewer work at speed without reconstructing context

contentSections.title: What a cold reviewer actually starts with

contentSections.body: You spend an afternoon going back and forth with an assistant, trying three approaches before landing on one. You open a PR: "Fixes pricing bug." The reviewer opens it five minutes later, knowing none of that afternoon, looking at a diff that makes sense only in light of the two approaches you already ruled out.

contentSections.scenario: Two PRs land the same day, same size, same actual quality of code. PR A: "Fixes pricing bug." PR B: "Bulk discounts were applying before the loyalty discount instead of after, letting a $100 item with both discounts go to $58 instead of the correct $62. Swapped the order in calculateFinalPrice; added a test asserting discount order for a case with both discounts active."
contentSections.question: Which PR gets a better review, and why?

options.label: PR B — the reviewer knows exactly what to verify before reading a line of diff
PR A — shorter descriptions are read faster, so review is quicker
Neither — review quality depends only on the code, not the description

feedback.b: Right. The reviewer of PR B already knows the bug, the fix mechanism, and what a correct test should assert — they can check the diff against a clear claim instead of reconstructing what happened from scratch. That's a faster *and* more accurate review, not just a faster one.
feedback.a: PR A is faster to read and slower to review — the reviewer now has to infer the bug from the diff itself, which takes longer than reading four sentences and is more likely to miss something.
feedback.neither: The code being identical is exactly what isolates the variable: same code, radically different review quality, because the description is doing real work that the code alone can't do.

contentSections.concept: A PR description is not documentation of a decision already made — it's the interface the reviewer works through. Everything you know that isn't in the description, the reviewer doesn't have. That's true of any PR, but it's sharper for AI-assisted changes: the exploratory back-and-forth that produced the final diff happened in a conversation the reviewer never sees, so if it isn't distilled into the description, it's simply gone from the reviewer's side.

contentSections.body: The description's job is narrow and specific: give a reviewer, who was in none of the conversations that produced this diff, enough to review it at the same depth you could review it yourself. Not the full story — a reviewer doesn't need to know you tried three approaches — but the *result* of that process: what changed, why, what's been checked, and what deserves a closer look. Everything else is left for the diff to show.

contentSections.question: A reviewer without any description spends their first several minutes on a PR doing what, exactly?
contentSections.answer: Reconstructing what you already knew before you opened the PR — what the bug or goal was, what approach was taken and why, and what's already been tested — by reverse-engineering it from the diff alone, which is slower and more error-prone than you writing four sentences.
contentSections.hint: They're not reading code yet. What are they trying to figure out first?

contentSections.body: The description is the interface the reviewer works through — everything you know that isn't in it, they don't have.

contentSections.title: What actually belongs in it

contentSections.body: Not every PR needs three paragraphs. A one-line typo fix needs one line. The skill is knowing which of these four things a *given* change actually requires, and writing exactly that — no more, no less.

contentSections.scenario: You're writing the description for a PR that changes how failed payment retries are scheduled — from a fixed 3-retry, 5-second-apart pattern to exponential backoff capped at 5 attempts.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in the description? Select all that apply.

items.label: Why the change was made — what problem the fixed pattern was causing
What was tested — which scenarios, and how
The full history of every approach considered and rejected before this one
What deserves a close look — e.g. the backoff cap interacting with an existing rate limiter

explanation.why: Essential — without it, a reviewer can't judge whether exponential backoff is actually the right fix for the underlying problem, only whether the code correctly implements *some* backoff.
explanation.tested: Essential — tells the reviewer what's already verified so they know where their own checking is still needed.
explanation.history: Not needed, and actively counterproductive — a reviewer doesn't need the two rejected approaches, and including them adds reading time without adding anything they can act on.
explanation.focus: Essential, and often the highest-value sentence in the whole description — it routes the reviewer's limited attention to the one interaction most likely to have a subtle bug.

contentSections.synthesis: Three things earn their place: why, what's tested, and what to focus on. The full decision history doesn't — that's useful in a design doc or a conversation, not in the thing a reviewer reads to decide whether 40 lines of retry logic are correct.

contentSections.body: Why, what's tested, and what to focus on — that's the whole list. Everything else is the diff's job to show.

title: Splitting a large generated change into reviewable pieces
description: How to turn one 900-line generated diff into a stack of PRs a human can actually hold in their head — split by dependency, not by file type, so each piece is independently reviewable and mergeable.

learningObjectives.text: Split a large generated change into independently reviewable, dependency-ordered pieces
Separate an intended change from incidental scope an assistant added along the way

contentSections.title: Why size alone breaks review

contentSections.body: An assistant asked to "add saved searches" doesn't stop at the smallest useful unit — it writes the migration, the endpoint, the permissions check and the frontend component in one pass, because nothing told it to stop sooner. The result is technically one feature and practically un-reviewable as one PR.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer opens a 900-line PR at 4:45pm. By 5:15 they've approved it with two minor comments on variable names.
contentSections.question: What actually happened to the review, mechanically?

options.label: Human working memory can't hold 900 lines of unfamiliar logic at once, so attention collapsed onto the easiest-to-spot issues
The reviewer is simply not a careful person
900 lines is actually a normal, manageable size to review properly

feedback.memory: Right — this isn't a character flaw, it's a working-memory limit. Nobody holds a migration, an endpoint's permission logic, and a frontend component's state handling in their head simultaneously with equal attention. What's left over goes to whatever's easiest to notice — a variable name — not necessarily what matters most.
feedback.carelessness: It's tempting to read it that way, but the same reviewer would likely catch real issues in a 150-line PR on the same feature area. The size itself is doing the damage, not the person.
feedback.normal: 900 lines across four different concerns (schema, API contract, permissions, UI) is well past what most reviewers can hold in working memory at matched depth — even skilled, careful reviewers default to skimming past a certain size.

contentSections.mechanism: Review quality doesn't degrade gracefully with size — it falls off a cliff once a diff exceeds what a person can hold in working memory, and everyone's cliff is roughly the same height regardless of skill or diligence. A four-concern, 900-line PR isn't four times harder to review than a 225-line one; it's a fundamentally different, much worse task, because the reviewer can no longer attend to all four concerns at once.

contentSections.body: The fix isn't reviewing more carefully — it's changing what gets reviewed at once. **Split by dependency, not by file type or by concern-that-sounds-tidy.** A migration, then the endpoint that needs it, then the frontend that calls the endpoint — each one reviewable and mergeable on its own, each one testable against something real rather than a stub. Splitting by file type ("all the backend changes," "all the frontend changes") looks organized but doesn't reduce cognitive load the same way, because each piece still requires understanding the whole feature to judge whether it's right.

contentSections.question: A generated change adds a `notification_preferences` table, an endpoint to update it, and a settings-page UI that calls the endpoint — plus, unprompted, the assistant also renamed a `notif_type` column used by three unrelated existing features. Order the actual splitting decisions you'd make.
steps: Pull the unrelated column rename into its own separate PR (or drop it) — it's not part of this feature and has its own blast radius
Open the migration PR for the new table alone
Open the endpoint PR, built against the now-merged migration
Open the UI PR, built against the now-merged endpoint
contentSections.explanation: The rename has to be pulled out first because it's not actually part of the feature — it's incidental scope the assistant added while it was in the file, and it touches three unrelated features' blast radius, which deserves its own focused review completely separate from saved-notification-preferences. Once that's separated, the remaining three pieces follow the same dependency order as any layered feature: schema, then the thing that needs the schema, then the thing that needs that.

contentSections.body: Split by what depends on what, not by what kind of file changed — and pull out anything the assistant did that you didn't actually ask for.

contentSections.title: Making the split actually mergeable

contentSections.body: A stack of PRs that all sit open waiting for each other isn't better than one big PR — it just moves the bottleneck. Each piece needs to be genuinely independently mergeable, which means it needs to work, and be tested, on its own.

contentSections.code:
PR 1: adds `saved_searches` table (migration only)
PR 2: adds POST /saved-searches and GET /saved-searches endpoints
PR 3: adds frontend "Save this search" button and results list

PR 2's tests: none included — "will test once the frontend is in so I can test end-to-end"
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this stack?

options.label: PR 2 isn't actually independently mergeable — it has no way to verify correctness without PR 3 existing
There should be more than three PRs
The migration should come after the endpoint

feedback.not-independent: Right. "I'll test once the frontend exists" means PR 2 can't actually be verified correct on its own — a reviewer approving it is taking the endpoint's correctness on faith, which defeats the point of splitting in the first place. The endpoint should have its own tests (calling it directly, not through UI) before it merges.
feedback.too-few: Three is a reasonable split for this feature's actual dependency structure — the problem isn't the count, it's that PR 2 can't stand on its own.
feedback.order: The order is right — a migration has to exist before anything can be built against the table it creates.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Independently mergeable means independently *verifiable*, not just independently deployable. If a piece's correctness can only be confirmed once a later piece exists, it isn't really split — it's just one PR's review deferred to when a different PR merges. Each PR in a stack needs its own tests against its own claims: the endpoint PR asserts what the endpoint returns for given inputs, tested by calling the endpoint directly, with no dependency on the UI that will eventually call it.

contentSections.body: A useful check before opening a stack: could each PR be reviewed, tested, and merged even if every PR after it in the stack were deleted right now? If the answer is no for any of them, that piece isn't actually split — it's just been renamed. This is also where labs and reviewable stacks connect to the testing discipline from the previous module: each PR needs its own tests proving its own claim, the same way a strengthened test suite needs a case for every claim it makes.
A stack only works if every piece in it is independently verifiable — not just independently named.

title: Disclosing what was generated, and why it matters to the reviewer
description: Disclosure isn't a confession — it's information that changes how a reviewer should calibrate their scrutiny, and it works best when it names what was generated, what was checked, and where to look closest.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate what a disclosure statement needs to contain to be useful to a reviewer
Explain why generated code's failure pattern differs from a careful human author's

contentSections.title: What disclosure is actually for

contentSections.body: "AI-assisted" is on almost every PR at this point and tells a reviewer nothing they didn't already assume. The question worth asking isn't whether to disclose — it's what disclosure needs to say to actually change how someone reviews.

contentSections.scenario: A PR adds rate-limiting middleware. Two versions of a disclosure note sit at the top: Version A says "AI-assisted." Version B says "First draft generated; I reviewed and adjusted the retry-after calculation specifically — that's the part I'm least certain about."
contentSections.question: Which version actually changes what the reviewer does?

options.label: B — it names a specific place to focus attention
A — any AI involvement is the important signal
Neither — reviewers should read every line equally regardless of disclosure

feedback.b: Right. B tells the reviewer exactly where the author's own confidence is lowest, which is where a reviewer's limited attention produces the most value. That's actionable in a way 'AI-assisted' isn't.
feedback.a: Nearly every PR at this point involves AI somewhere, so this flag has stopped carrying information — it doesn't distinguish this PR from any other, and doesn't tell the reviewer where to look.
feedback.neither: In principle, equal scrutiny everywhere sounds rigorous, but nobody actually reviews that way — attention is finite and gets allocated somehow. Disclosure that names a specific weak point directs that allocation on purpose instead of by accident.

contentSections.concept: Disclosure isn't a moral confession, it's a routing signal. A reviewer's attention is a limited resource; a disclosure statement that says what was generated, what was checked, and what's least certain spends that resource where it does the most good. A generic "AI-assisted" spends it nowhere, because it doesn't distinguish anything.

contentSections.body: The reason this matters more than it might seem: generated code has a specific failure pattern that differs from a careful human author's. It tends to be **locally plausible and fluent even when subtly wrong** — a validation regex that looks right and rejects a valid edge case, an off-by-one that reads naturally in context. A skilled human making a mistake often leaves a rougher edge that draws the eye; a fluent generated mistake usually doesn't. A reviewer who doesn't know this reviews at their normal calibration; a reviewer who does knows to specifically hunt for the smooth-looking wrong answer, not just the rough one.

contentSections.question: Why is it usually a mistake to disclose generation as a form of covering yourself — "AI wrote it, not my fault if it's wrong" — rather than as routing information?
contentSections.answer: Because it doesn't change what the reviewer does with the information — it just relocates blame instead of directing attention. The PR still needs review either way; framing disclosure as liability-management rather than "here's what to check closely" throws away the actual value disclosure has, which is focusing the reviewer's limited attention where the author's confidence is lowest.
contentSections.hint: Does a defensive disclosure statement tell the reviewer anything they can act on?

contentSections.body: Disclosure earns its place by naming what to check, not by naming that AI was involved somewhere.

contentSections.title: Calibrating a reviewer's scrutiny with it

contentSections.body: The most useful disclosure statements aren't longer — they're more specific. "Generated, lightly reviewed, I'm not confident about the concurrency handling" is four extra words past "generated" and it's doing almost all the work.

contentSections.scenario: Rank these disclosure statements for a PR that adds a background job processing refunds.
contentSections.question: Which of these give a reviewer something they can actually act on? Select all that apply.

items.label: "Generated with heavy review — I traced every branch against the refund state machine by hand and I'm confident in it"
"AI wrote most of this"
"Generated, lightly reviewed — I have not verified what happens if the job is interrupted mid-refund and retried"
"Should be fine, the AI is usually pretty good at this stuff"

explanation.a: Tells the reviewer the author already did serious verification, which can reasonably shift some of their scrutiny elsewhere — that's actionable.
explanation.b: Generic, no confidence level, no focus point — carries no information a reviewer can use to calibrate anything.
explanation.c: Names the exact unverified case (interrupted-and-retried) — this is the single most useful sentence a reviewer could get, because it's precisely where a background refund job is most likely to have a real bug (double-refunding).
explanation.d: This is a vibe, not information — 'usually pretty good' says nothing about this specific change.

contentSections.synthesis: The two useful statements share a shape: they name a confidence level *and* a specific thing that was or wasn't checked. The two useless ones name that AI was involved and stop there, which by itself has become nearly zero-information in 2026.

contentSections.body: A disclosure statement earns its keep the same way a PR description does: by naming something specific, not by existing.

title: Responding to review on code you didn't write
description: How to answer a reviewer's question about a decision an assistant made without either hiding behind "the AI did it" or bluffing confidence you don't have — by finding out the real answer and owning it.

learningObjectives.text: Respond accountably to review feedback on generated code, including decisions the author can't immediately explain
Distinguish an accountable response from deflection or unearned confidence

contentSections.title: Owning a decision you didn't personally make

contentSections.body: A reviewer asks why a retry loop backs off exponentially, capped at 30 seconds, instead of retrying at a fixed 5-second interval. You genuinely don't remember choosing that number — you asked an assistant for "a sensible retry with backoff" and it picked 30. The honest answer right now is: you don't know.

contentSections.scenario: Three possible replies to the reviewer's question about the 30-second cap: (1) "That's just what the AI generated, not sure why 30." (2) "30 seconds is definitely the right number for this." (3) "Good question — let me check whether 30s is tied to anything specific downstream and get back to you."
contentSections.question: Which reply treats this the way you'd treat a decision a human teammate made that you inherited and can't currently explain?

options.label: Reply 3 — investigate and report back with an actual answer
Reply 1 — accurately describe where the number came from
Reply 2 — project confidence so the review moves forward

feedback.3: Right. This is exactly what you'd do if a departed colleague had written this code and you inherited the review — find out whether the number is load-bearing or arbitrary, then answer with an actual finding instead of a guess or a shrug.
feedback.1: It's accurate, but it stops at description instead of moving to accountability — it tells the reviewer where the number came from and nothing about whether it's right, which is the actual question they asked.
feedback.2: Confidence without a reason behind it is worse than admitting uncertainty — if the reviewer presses ("why 30, specifically?") there's nothing behind the claim, and a wrong confident answer is more damaging to trust than an honest "let me check."

contentSections.concept: "I didn't write it" is true and not an answer to "is it right." The reviewer isn't asking about authorship, they're asking about a decision, and someone has to be accountable for that decision before the PR merges — which means finding out the real answer, the same way you would for any inherited code whose author isn't in the room to ask.

contentSections.body: This is the same discipline the module opened with, turned around: a test is a claim someone relies on; a code review response is also a claim someone relies on. "The AI wrote it that way" is not a claim about correctness — it's a non-answer wearing the shape of an answer. The accountable move costs a few minutes: check whether the number ties to something real (a downstream rate limit, a value used elsewhere in the codebase for a similar purpose) or is genuinely arbitrary, and say which one it turned out to be.

contentSections.problem: A reviewer comments on a generated function: "This retries on every exception type, including validation errors — shouldn't those fail immediately instead of retrying?" You hadn't considered the distinction.

steps.label: Don't answer immediately
steps.work: Resist the urge to defend the current behaviour or agree instantly without checking — both skip finding out what's actually true.
steps.why: A validation error retried five times before failing is a real bug (wasted time, delayed error to the user) if the reviewer's instinct is right, and worth five minutes to actually verify rather than guess about.

steps.label: Check what the code currently does
steps.work: Confirm: yes, the retry wraps a broad exception handler with no filtering by error type, so a validation error (which will never succeed on retry, by definition) gets the same 5-attempt backoff as a transient network error.
steps.why: This is the fact-finding step — same as checking whether the 30-second cap ties to something real. You need to know what's true before you can respond usefully.

steps.label: Confirm the reviewer's instinct is correct
steps.work: Validation errors are deterministic — retrying the exact same invalid input will fail the exact same way every time, so retrying just delays the failure without ever changing the outcome.
steps.why: This is the reasoning that makes the fix obviously correct, not just reviewer-suggested — worth stating explicitly so the fix isn't just deference.

steps.label: Reply with the finding and the fix
steps.work: "Good catch — confirmed, it currently retries validation errors too, which just delays a failure that was never going to succeed. Filtering those out to fail immediately, keeping retry for the transient cases (timeouts, 5xx responses)."
steps.why: This names what was found, agrees with actual reasoning behind it (not just "ok I'll change it"), and states the specific fix — the reviewer knows exactly what to expect in the next push.

faded.problem: A reviewer asks: "Why does this cache key include the user's timezone? Doesn't that mean two users in different timezones never share a cached result even for identical data?" You don't remember why the assistant included timezone in the key.

blanks.prompt: What's the first thing to do before replying? (a few words)
blanks.why: Same move as both worked examples — find out what's true before responding, rather than defending or immediately agreeing.

blanks.prompt: If timezone genuinely doesn't affect the cached data, what's the accountable reply? (state the finding + the fix, briefly)
blanks.answer: confirmed it's unnecessary, removing it from the key to improve cache hit rate
accept: you're right, removing timezone from the key
blanks.why: Same shape as the retry example: name the finding, then the specific fix — not just 'ok, changing it.'

blanks.prompt: If it turns out timezone-sensitive data (like a 'today's deals' list) actually is in the cached payload, what should the reply do instead? (a few words)
blanks.answer: explain why it's needed and keep it
accept: explain the reason and keep it as is
blanks.why: The accountable response isn't always 'change it because they asked' — sometimes the finding is that the original decision was actually right, and the reply should say why.

contentSections.procedure: **Don't defend or concede on reflex → check what's actually true → reply with the finding and a specific next step.** The finding might vindicate the original code or might not — the accountable part is that you found out, not that you agreed.

contentSections.body: "The AI wrote it" describes where the code came from. The reviewer asked whether it's right. Those need different answers.

contentSections.title: When you genuinely can't verify

contentSections.body: Sometimes checking takes real effort — a distributed system's edge case, a load-bearing decision buried three services away. It's fine to not have the answer in the moment. It's not fine to pretend you do.

contentSections.question: Between silence, a confident guess, and "I don't know yet, here's how I'll find out, here's when" — which is the worst response to leave a reviewer with, and why?
contentSections.answer: A confident guess is worst. Silence at least signals nothing is being hidden — the reviewer knows to follow up. A wrong confident answer gets trusted and acted on, which is more damaging than either being asked again or waiting a day for a real answer.
contentSections.hint: Which one actively misleads the reviewer into trusting something that might be false?

contentSections.body: The honest version of "I don't know yet" is a complete, professional reply on its own: name what you don't know, say how you'll find out, and give a timeframe. "I don't know why 30 seconds specifically — checking whether it ties to the downstream service's rate limit, will confirm by end of day" is a fine thing to post. What isn't fine is silence (the reviewer is left hanging, unsure if they were heard) or a guess dressed as certainty (the reviewer now trusts an answer that might be wrong, which is worse than trusting nothing).
An honest "I don't know yet, here's how I'll find out" is a complete answer. A confident guess is not.

title: Reviewing someone else's AI-assisted pull request
description: What changes about reviewing when you know the change was generated — which checks are the same as any review, and which specifically target the failure pattern of fluent-but-wrong generated code.

learningObjectives.text: Calibrate review depth to a change's disclosed provenance and stakes
Identify review checks that specifically target generated code's failure pattern versus general good practice

contentSections.title: The two kinds of check

contentSections.body: Reviewing a teammate's AI-assisted PR isn't a different skill from reviewing any PR — most of it is the same. But part of it should specifically hunt for the way generated code tends to be wrong, which is a different shape of mistake than the ones a careful senior engineer usually makes.

contentSections.scenario: You're reviewing a teammate's PR adding email validation to a signup form, disclosed as "generated, light review." The regex looks reasonable: `^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$`.
contentSections.question: What's the specific thing worth checking, given the disclosure, that a confident-looking regex like this might hide?

options.label: Whether it rejects valid addresses it looks like it should accept — e.g. a plus-addressed email like name+tag@domain.com
Whether the variable is named appropriately
Whether the code is formatted per the linter config

feedback.plus: Right — this regex actually does accept plus-addressing here (the `[^\s@]+` before the @ allows it), but the habit of checking is the point: a regex that *looks* thorough and handles the obvious cases can still reject a real, valid pattern nobody thought to try, and that's exactly the kind of fluent-but-subtly-wrong mistake generated code tends to make.
feedback.naming: Worth checking in any review, but it's not the check that's specifically sharpened by knowing this was generated with light review.
feedback.formatting: A linter catches this automatically in most setups — it's not where a human reviewer's judgment adds value, generated or not.

contentSections.concept: Generated code passes a casual read more often than it should, because it's fluent by construction — it looks like code a competent person wrote, which is exactly why a reviewer's normal pattern-matching ("this looks like reasonable code") is less reliable here than usual. The specific check worth adding isn't "is this bad code" — it usually isn't — it's "does this handle a case that looks like it's covered but actually isn't."

contentSections.body: Most of a normal review still applies unchanged: does it do what the description says, is it tested, does it introduce a security or data issue, is it consistent with how the rest of the codebase does this. What's worth adding, specifically because of the disclosure, is a deliberate pass for **plausible-looking-but-wrong**: an edge case that reads as handled but isn't, a value that looks intentional but was never verified, logic that quietly reinvents something that already exists elsewhere in the codebase instead of reusing it.
