contentSections.question: Why is 'quietly reinventing existing logic instead of reusing it' specifically a generated-code risk, more than a human-written-code risk?
contentSections.answer: A human writing new code in a codebase they know tends to remember "we already have a function for this" and reach for it. An assistant working from the immediate context of a prompt and a file has no equivalent memory of the rest of the codebase unless it's explicitly shown — so it's structurally more likely to write a plausible-looking reimplementation of something that already exists, silently diverging from it over time.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a human author remembers by default that an assistant working from a narrower context window doesn't.

contentSections.body: Most of the review is unchanged. The part worth sharpening is the hunt for confident-looking code that's wrong in a way a casual read won't catch.

contentSections.title: Calibrating depth to stakes and disclosure

contentSections.body: Not every generated PR deserves the same scrutiny. A typo fix and a payment retry handler disclosed the same way don't earn the same review depth — stakes and disclosure combine, they don't override each other.

contentSections.scenario: Four PRs land in your queue, all disclosed as "generated, light review": (A) fixes a typo in a help-page tooltip. (B) changes how failed payment retries are scheduled. (C) adds a new CSS utility class. (D) adds a permissions check to an internal admin tool.
contentSections.question: Which of these deserve deeper-than-default scrutiny specifically because of the disclosure plus their stakes? Select all that apply.

items.label: Typo fix in a tooltip
Payment retry scheduling
New CSS utility class
Permissions check on an admin tool

explanation.a: Low stakes, easy to verify correct on sight — a light-review disclosure doesn't change much here because there's very little for a subtle bug to hide in.
explanation.b: High stakes (money, retries can double-charge if wrong) and the exact kind of logic (edge cases, timing) where a fluent-but-wrong mistake is easy to miss on a skim — deserves real attention.
explanation.c: Low stakes and low complexity — a wrong CSS class is visually obvious and cheap to fix, not the profile of a change that needs deep scrutiny.
explanation.d: High stakes — a subtly wrong permissions check is a security hole, and 'light review' plus 'permissions logic' is exactly the combination from lesson three's stacking-signals point.

contentSections.synthesis: Disclosure tells you the author's own confidence; stakes tell you what a mistake costs. Neither alone tells you how hard to look — it's the combination, the same calibration lesson three introduced from the reviewer's side, now applied by you as the one doing the reviewing.

contentSections.body: Disclosure and stakes combine to set review depth — a light-review tag on a low-stakes change needs less scrutiny than the same tag on a payment or permissions change.

title: Practice — Rewrite Seven Pull Request Descriptions for a Cold Reviewer
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: take a thin or misleading PR description and turn it into one that actually equips a reviewer who wasn't there for any of the work.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the what/why/tested/focus structure to weak PR descriptions at speed

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Same skill as the lessons, seven fresh descriptions to fix. One sitting or several — nothing here expires.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for on the checkpoint.

title: Lab — Split and Describe a 900-Line Generated Change
description: Take one large, described-in-plain-language generated change and turn it into a stack of independently mergeable, independently described pull requests a real reviewer could work through.

learningObjectives.text: Split a large generated change into dependency-ordered, independently reviewable pieces
Write a description for each piece that equips a cold reviewer without requiring the others

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the module's real test: not writing good code, but turning one large generated change into something a real, busy, cold reviewer could actually work through piece by piece.

contentSections.title: Split and describe a 900-line generated change
contentSections.brief: An assistant was asked to "add a bulk CSV export feature to the admin dashboard" and produced roughly 900 lines: a background job that generates the CSV, a new API endpoint to trigger and poll the job, a permissions check restricting it to admin roles, a frontend button and progress indicator, and — unprompted — a refactor of an unrelated date-formatting utility it decided to "clean up" while it was in that file. Turn this into a stack of PRs a real reviewer could work through.
contentSections.deliverable: A stack of reviewable pull requests — as titles, descriptions, and a stated dependency order — each independently mergeable, each with its own description covering why, what was tested, and what to focus on.

stages.title: Separate the intended feature from incidental scope
stages.instructions: Identify the unrelated date-formatting refactor as incidental scope, not part of the requested feature. Decide and state whether it becomes its own separate PR or gets dropped from this change entirely — and why.
stages.checkpoint: You have an explicit decision, with a stated reason, about the unrelated refactor — not left bundled in by default.

stages.title: Determine the dependency order of the real feature's pieces
stages.instructions: List the remaining pieces (background job, endpoint, permissions check, frontend) and order them by what depends on what — the same reasoning as lesson two's worked example. Decide whether the permissions check belongs bundled with the endpoint or as its own PR, and state why.
stages.checkpoint: You have a stated order with a one-sentence reason for each piece's position, including your call on where the permissions check lives.

stages.title: Write each PR's title and description
stages.instructions: For each PR in your stack (the incidental-refactor decision from stage 1 plus the ordered pieces from stage 2), write a title and a description covering: what changed, why, what was tested (state a plausible, specific test approach for each piece — you don't need to write real code), and what a reviewer should look at most closely.
stages.checkpoint: Every PR in the stack has all four elements, and none of them assumes the reviewer has read the others.

stages.title: Self-check independence
stages.instructions: For each PR, ask: could this be reviewed, tested, and merged if every PR after it in the stack were deleted right now? Where the answer is no, fix the description or the split until it's yes — the way lesson two's spot-flaw example required the endpoint PR to have its own tests rather than deferring to the frontend.
stages.checkpoint: Every PR in the stack passes the 'delete everything after it' test, or you've documented the one genuine exception and why it's unavoidable.

rubric.criterion: Incidental scope was deliberately separated, not bundled by default
rubric.meets: The unrelated date-formatting refactor has an explicit decision (own PR or dropped) with a stated reason, not silently left inside a feature PR.
Each PR only depends on PRs earlier in the stack, and the reasoning for the order is stated, not just asserted.

rubric.criterion: Every PR description has why, tested, and focus
rubric.meets: All four elements (what, why, tested, focus) are present for every PR, written for a reader who hasn't seen the others.
Every PR passes, or explicitly and justifiably fails, the 'delete everything after it' independence test from stage 4.
No description could be copy-pasted onto a different PR without changes — every sentence is about this specific change.

contentSections.body: A stack of PRs is only as good as its weakest link's independence — one piece that secretly depends on a later one breaks the whole point of splitting.

title: Checkpoint — Review Workflow and PR Craft
description: Ten questions: five from this module, five pulling back to Tests You Can Trust. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions and last module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Review Workflow and PR Craft

questions.from: This module — The pull request description as the reviewer's only context
questions.prompt: What does a cold reviewer know that only the PR description can tell them?

options.label: Everything the author knows that isn't visible in the diff itself — why, what's tested, what to focus on
The exact line count of the change
Nothing — the diff alone is always sufficient

questions.explanation: The description is the interface for everything the author knows that the diff can't show on its own — reasoning, verification, and where attention should go.

questions.from: This module — Splitting a large generated change into reviewable pieces
questions.prompt: Why split a large change by dependency order rather than by file type?

options.label: So each piece is independently verifiable against something real, not a stub
It produces fewer total PRs
File-type splits are against most teams' conventions

questions.explanation: Dependency order is what makes each PR testable and reviewable against real, already-merged pieces — a file-type split still requires understanding the whole feature to judge any one part.

questions.from: This module — Disclosing what was generated, and why it matters to the reviewer
questions.prompt: What makes a disclosure statement actually useful to a reviewer?

options.label: It names what was generated, what was checked, and where confidence is lowest
It simply states that AI was involved
It apologizes for using AI assistance

questions.explanation: A generic 'AI-assisted' carries almost no information anymore — the useful version routes the reviewer's attention to a specific place.

questions.from: This module — Responding to review on code you didn't write
questions.prompt: A reviewer questions a decision in generated code you can't currently explain. What's the accountable response?

options.label: Say you don't know, then find out whether the decision is load-bearing or arbitrary, and report back
Say "the AI generated it that way" and move on
Defend it confidently to keep the review moving

questions.explanation: "The AI wrote it" describes provenance, not correctness — the reviewer asked about correctness, which requires actually finding out.

questions.from: This module — Reviewing someone else's AI-assisted pull request
questions.prompt: What review check is specifically sharpened by knowing a change was generated?

options.label: Hunting for a case that looks handled but isn't, since generated code is fluent even when subtly wrong
Checking variable naming conventions
Checking that the linter passes

questions.explanation: Naming and linting matter in any review — the check that's specifically sharpened here is the hunt for plausible-looking-but-wrong logic, because generated code tends to read as competently done even when it's not.

questions.from: Previous module — A test is a claim about behaviour someone will rely on
questions.prompt: What makes a test a claim someone can rely on, rather than decoration?

options.label: It asserts a specific expected outcome that would change if the code were wrong
It has a descriptive name
It runs fast

questions.explanation: A fast, well-named test that only checks 'didn't throw' still can't distinguish correct behaviour from most kinds of wrong behaviour.

questions.from: Previous module — Specifying tests instead of asking for "some tests"
questions.prompt: What's missing from a vague request like "test the rate limiter" that a specified one supplies?

options.label: The specific cases that matter and the expected outcome for each
A longer prompt in general
A request to avoid AI assistance

questions.explanation: Length isn't the point — naming cases and expected outcomes is what removes the guesswork.

questions.from: Previous module — The cases a generated suite always misses
questions.prompt: Why does a suite generated by reading an implementation tend to miss malformed or empty input?

options.label: The implementation gives no hint that such input might occur, so nothing prompts a test for it
Models can't write tests for edge cases at all
Malformed input never actually happens in production

questions.explanation: A suite derived from reading code inherits that code's own blind spots — this is structural, not a quality issue with any particular model.

questions.from: Previous module — Mutation thinking: would this test notice?
questions.prompt: What does mutation thinking check that code coverage numbers don't?

options.label: Whether a test would actually fail if the code were deliberately made wrong
How many lines of code ran during the test
How long the test suite takes to run

questions.explanation: Coverage tracks whether a line executed; mutation thinking tracks whether anything would notice if that line's logic were wrong — a much stronger and different claim.

questions.from: Previous module — Fast, deterministic, and independent — or nobody runs them
questions.prompt: What's the realistic long-run effect of a test that fails for unrelated reasons about 1 time in 20?

options.label: People learn to distrust red builds and start re-running or ignoring failures, including real ones
No effect, since it's rare
The team immediately deletes the whole suite

questions.explanation: The real cost isn't the occasional false failure — it's what that trains people to do the next time any test fails.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back today returns in a later checkpoint — that's the design.

title: It works here: the environment you forgot you had
description: Why a build that works on the machine that wrote it can still be broken — because it's depending on something that machine has and quietly never wrote down.

learningObjectives.text: Identify environment assumptions a build silently depends on but never declares
Explain why CI's clean environment surfaces assumptions a local machine hides

contentSections.title: The dependency nobody declared

contentSections.body: A generated deploy script calls `convert` to resize an uploaded image. It works instantly on the author's laptop. It fails in CI with `command not found: convert`. Nothing in the project asked for ImageMagick — the author installed it eleven months ago for an unrelated side project and forgot it was there.

contentSections.scenario: A `Makefile` target runs `jq '.version' package.json` to read a version string during the build. It's never listed as a project dependency anywhere.
contentSections.question: Why does this work for three of four teammates and fail for the fourth?

options.label: The fourth teammate's machine doesn't happen to have jq installed globally
Their package.json is formatted differently
jq only works on certain operating systems

feedback.missing: Right — jq is a real, useful tool that a lot of developers happen to have installed for unrelated reasons, which makes it an easy one to silently depend on without ever declaring it. The fourth teammate simply never installed it, and nothing about the project told them they needed to.
feedback.format: package.json's format isn't the variable here — jq would fail the same way (not found) regardless of what's inside the file, because the tool itself is what's missing.
feedback.os: jq runs on all major platforms — this isn't an OS compatibility issue, it's a 'was this ever installed on this specific machine' issue.

contentSections.concept: A build 'working' on a given machine is really a claim about that machine's accumulated state — every tool anyone ever installed on it, for any reason, at any point in the past. None of that state is visible from the project's own files unless it's explicitly declared there. CI's environment starts from nothing every time, which is exactly what makes it the place these undeclared assumptions get caught — not a flaw in CI, but the first honest test the project has had.

contentSections.body: This is worth internalizing as a reframe: **CI failing when local succeeds is not CI being difficult — it's CI being honest.** Your laptop has years of accumulated global installs, cached tools, and environment quirks that make it a uniquely bad predictor of what a stranger's machine, or a fresh CI container, actually needs to run this project. The goal isn't to make CI more like your laptop; it's to make the project's declared requirements complete enough that a machine with nothing pre-installed can still build it.

contentSections.question: Name one category of thing, besides command-line tools like ImageMagick or jq, that a project can silently depend on without declaring it anywhere.
contentSections.answer: A specific runtime version (Node, Python, a language toolchain), an environment variable the author set once in their shell profile and forgot about, or an OS-level library the language's package manager doesn't track (image codecs, database client libraries) — any of these can be present on the author's machine by accident and absent everywhere else.
contentSections.hint: Think beyond command-line tools — versions, environment variables, and system libraries all work the same way.

contentSections.body: A build that only works on the machine that wrote it isn't working — it's borrowing that machine's history without saying so.

contentSections.title: Spotting the gap before CI does

contentSections.body: Waiting for CI to fail is the expensive way to find an undeclared dependency — it costs a round trip and someone else's confusion. A faster check exists: read the project's setup instructions as if you'd never touched this machine before.

contentSections.scenario: A generated README says: "Clone the repo, run npm install, run npm start." A new contributor follows it exactly and gets `Error: Cannot find module 'sharp'` — a native image library that requires a system-level build toolchain the README never mentions.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind this failure?

options.label: sharp needs native compilation tools present on the system that npm install alone doesn't guarantee or install
The new contributor typed a command wrong
sharp is broken and needs to be replaced

feedback.native: Right. Some packages compile native code during install and need system-level build tools (a C compiler, specific headers) present — tools the original author likely already had installed for unrelated reasons, the same pattern as ImageMagick. npm install can fail partway through this compilation step with an error that looks unrelated to the real cause.
feedback.typo: The instructions were followed exactly — this isn't a user error, it's a real gap in what the README declared as required.
feedback.broken: sharp works fine on machines with the right build tools present — the package isn't broken, the documented setup is incomplete.

contentSections.mechanism: Native dependencies are a sharper version of the same problem: a package manager's install step can itself silently depend on system-level tools that were never the responsibility of `npm install` to provide, and were present on the original author's machine by accident. The failure surfaces as a confusing error deep in an install log, which is much harder to diagnose than a clean 'command not found.'

contentSections.body: A cheap habit that catches most of this early: describe your own setup steps to a version of yourself with a completely fresh machine, and notice every place you'd silently reach for something already installed. Better still, actually try it — a fresh container, a spare machine, or even a temporary new user account — before assuming "it works" means the project is actually reproducible rather than just familiar to the one machine that's run it the longest.
The fastest way to find an undeclared dependency is to try the setup on a machine that's never seen this project before — not to wait for CI to find it for you.

title: Lockfiles, pinned versions, and reproducible installs
description: Why a version range in a manifest file is a promise about the future, not a fact about the present — and how a lockfile turns 'probably the same' into 'exactly the same.'

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a version range permits versus what a lockfile records
Configure an install process to actually honor a committed lockfile

contentSections.title: What a version range actually promises

contentSections.body: `"date-utils": "^2.1.0"` looks pinned. It isn't. It's a promise that any 2.x.x release is acceptable, and every fresh install is free to pick whichever one is newest at that exact moment — which means two installs of the identical project, weeks apart, can legitimately end up running different code.

contentSections.scenario: A generated `package.json` for a new service lists every dependency with a caret range (`^1.4.2`, `^3.0.1`, and so on) and no lockfile is committed to the repository.
contentSections.question: What happens when this project is deployed to production six weeks after it was last tested, with a fresh install as part of the deploy?

options.label: The deploy installs whatever the newest compatible versions are at that moment, which may not be what was tested
Nothing changes — caret ranges always resolve to the same version once set
The deploy fails outright since six weeks is too long

feedback.drift: Right. Six weeks is plenty of time for several dependencies to publish new compatible versions, and a fresh install with no lockfile will happily pick them up — meaning production is now running code that was never actually tested, resolved fresh at deploy time from ranges that were only ever meant as *compatibility* promises, not exact specifications.
feedback.same: Caret ranges are explicitly designed to allow movement within a major version — that's the whole point of using `^` instead of an exact version number. They will resolve differently as new compatible versions publish.
feedback.fails: Nothing about the passage of time makes an install fail on its own — it succeeds, just potentially with different resolved versions than last time, which is the more dangerous outcome because nothing visibly breaks to alert anyone.

contentSections.concept: A version range in a manifest describes what's *allowed*, not what actually ran. "Tested with whatever ^2.1.0 resolved to on a Tuesday in March" and "tested with 2.1.0 specifically" are different claims, and the range alone can't tell you which one you're getting on any given install. A lockfile is the artifact that captures the second, stronger claim.

contentSections.body: A lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, `poetry.lock`, and their equivalents in other ecosystems) records the exact resolved version tree from a real install — not just top-level dependencies but every transitive one, several layers deep, that a range alone would leave to be re-resolved each time. Committing it to version control means every future install, on any machine, reads the same exact tree instead of re-deriving one from ranges that keep drifting forward as new versions publish.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in order to actually get reproducible installs for a project that currently has no committed lockfile.
steps: Run a real install once, locally, to generate the lockfile from the current version ranges
Commit the generated lockfile to version control
Change the CI pipeline's install step to a strict, lockfile-respecting command instead of a plain range-resolving one
Confirm a second install, from the committed lockfile, resolves to the identical versions as the first
contentSections.explanation: You need a lockfile to exist before you can commit it, so generating it comes first. Committing it without changing the install command still leaves the door open for a range-resolving install to silently drift past it — the install command has to actually be told to respect the lockfile strictly. The last step is the actual proof: an install from the lockfile alone, with no ranges re-resolved, should reproduce the exact same versions, which is the property the whole exercise was for.

contentSections.body: A version range is what's allowed to install. A lockfile is what actually did — commit the second one, and use a command that respects it.

contentSections.title: Making the install step actually strict

contentSections.body: A committed lockfile that the install command is free to ignore is a lockfile in name only. This is the gap a lot of generated CI configs quietly leave open, because `npm install` and `npm ci` look almost interchangeable and aren't.

contentSections.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (relevant step)
- name: Install dependencies
  run: npm install

# package-lock.json is committed to the repo
contentSections.question: The lockfile is committed. What's still wrong with this CI step?

options.label: npm install can still resolve versions outside the lockfile based on package.json's ranges — it doesn't strictly enforce the lockfile
Nothing — a committed lockfile is enough on its own
The step needs to specify a Node version too, which is unrelated to the lockfile

feedback.not-strict: Right. `npm install` treats the lockfile as a hint, not a contract — if package.json's ranges permit something newer than what's in the lockfile, it can update the lockfile and install that instead. `npm ci` is the command that fails loudly if the lockfile and package.json don't agree, rather than quietly reconciling them.
feedback.nothing: The lockfile being present isn't the same as the install command being forced to honor it exactly — that's the actual gap here.
feedback.unrelated: Pinning a Node/runtime version is a real, separate concern worth having too, but it doesn't fix this specific gap — even with the right Node version, `npm install` can still drift from the lockfile.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is a one-word change: `npm ci` instead of `npm install`. `npm ci` deletes any existing `node_modules`, installs strictly from the lockfile, and fails immediately if the lockfile is missing or out of sync with `package.json` — exactly the strict, no-surprises behavior a CI pipeline should have, versus the flexible, developer-convenience behavior `npm install` is designed for on a local machine where you often *want* it to pick up new compatible versions.

contentSections.body: The same distinction exists across ecosystems under different names: Python's `pip install -r requirements.txt` versus a hash-locked install from `poetry.lock` or `pip-compile` output; Ruby's `bundle install` respecting `Gemfile.lock` strictly by default already, which is worth knowing as the exception rather than assuming every ecosystem behaves the same way. The pattern to check for, regardless of language: does the routine install command your CI runs treat the lockfile as authoritative, or as a suggestion it's allowed to update.
A committed lockfile only buys reproducibility if the install command is actually told to obey it strictly, not just read it.

title: Reading a CI failure that didn't happen locally
description: A short list of the actual usual suspects behind a CI-only failure — case sensitivity, timing, and environment differences — so a confusing red build becomes a specific hypothesis to check instead of a mystery.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a CI-only failure by matching its symptom to one of a small set of usual causes
Read a CI log for the specific evidence that distinguishes those causes

contentSections.title: The short list of usual suspects

contentSections.body: "It works locally" and a red CI build together feel like a contradiction. They aren't — CI and a local machine differ in a handful of specific, recurring ways, and almost every CI-only failure traces back to one of them.

contentSections.scenario: A React import reads `import Button from './Button'` and the file on disk is actually named `button.jsx`. It builds fine on the author's MacBook and fails in CI with `Module not found`.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism?

options.label: macOS's filesystem is case-insensitive by default; the Linux CI runner's isn't, so the mismatched casing only breaks on Linux
React doesn't work the same way in CI
CI has a slower disk, causing a timeout

feedback.case: Right — this is one of the single most common CI-only failures. macOS (and Windows) filesystems typically treat `Button` and `button` as the same file; Linux, which nearly all CI runners use, treats them as different files. The import was subtly wrong the whole time; only Linux was honest about it.
feedback.react: React's behavior doesn't differ by OS here — this is purely a filesystem lookup issue, before React ever gets involved.
feedback.slow: There's no timeout involved — the module genuinely isn't found under that exact casing on a case-sensitive filesystem, regardless of how fast the disk is.

contentSections.concept: Three categories cover most CI-only failures: **case sensitivity** (macOS/Windows forgive mismatched casing, Linux CI doesn't), **timing and ordering** (CI's parallelism or resource contention exposes races that rarely trigger in a single local run), and **environment differences** (locale, timezone, installed system packages, environment variables set locally and never declared). Naming which of the three you're looking at turns a vague 'CI is broken' into a specific, checkable hypothesis.

contentSections.body: The fastest diagnostic habit: read the error message for what it's actually claiming, not what it superficially resembles. "Module not found" almost always means a path or casing problem, not a real absence of the file. "Different result on repeated runs" almost always means timing or shared state, not a compiler bug. "Works alone, fails in the full suite" specifically isolates a state-sharing problem between tests, the same failure mode lesson four of the previous module covered from the test-writing side — now you're reading the log from the other end, as evidence instead of prevention.

contentSections.question: A CI log shows a date-formatting test failing with an unexpected format, and it never fails on any developer's local machine. Before reading the rest of this lesson: which of the three categories does this most likely belong to, and why?
contentSections.answer: Environment differences — specifically locale or timezone. CI containers often run with a different default locale (commonly a minimal 'C' locale) than a developer's own machine, which can format dates and numbers differently even though the code and the input are identical.
contentSections.hint: It's not about which files exist, and it's not about run order — what's different about the machine's own configured settings?

contentSections.body: Almost every CI-only failure sorts into case sensitivity, timing, or environment differences — naming which one turns confusion into a specific thing to check.

contentSections.title: Reading the log for the actual evidence

contentSections.body: Naming the category is only useful if you then go find the evidence in the log that confirms it, rather than guessing and re-running until something works — which is expensive and teaches you nothing for next time.

contentSections.problem: CI log excerpt: `FAIL tests/orderTotal.test.js — expected 42.50, received 42.49 (repeated across 3 CI runs, never fails locally)`. Diagnose it.

steps.label: Name the category from the symptom
steps.work: Same input, same code, different numeric result across environments — not a case-sensitivity symptom (no missing file), not obviously timing (it's deterministic-looking, always the same wrong value). Points toward an environment difference.
steps.why: Ruling categories in and out from the symptom's shape narrows the search before touching any code.

steps.label: Narrow to a specific environment difference
steps.work: A one-cent discrepancy in a total, consistent across runs, is a classic floating-point or rounding-mode symptom — worth checking whether the CI container's Node/language version, or a floating-point rounding setting, differs from local.
steps.why: Not every environment difference is locale — narrowing further based on the specific symptom (a one-cent gap, not a garbled format) points at a numeric precision issue rather than a display-formatting one.

steps.label: Check the actual versions
steps.work: Compare the exact runtime version pinned (or not pinned) in CI against what's installed locally — this connects directly back to lesson one's environment gap and lesson two's pinning discipline.
steps.why: If the runtime version isn't pinned, CI and local can genuinely be running different minor versions with different default floating-point behavior in edge cases.

steps.label: Confirm and fix at the source
steps.work: Once the version mismatch is confirmed, the real fix isn't patching the test's expected value — it's pinning the runtime version so local and CI are provably running the same one, closing the gap rather than working around its symptom.
steps.why: Patching the expected value to '42.49' would make the test pass without addressing why two supposedly-identical environments produce different arithmetic — the underlying reproducibility gap survives.

faded.problem: CI log: `FAIL tests/importCsv.test.js — Cannot find module './Parser'` (the file is actually `parser.js`). Passes locally on every developer's machine (all on macOS).

blanks.prompt: Which of the three categories does this belong to? (one or two words)
blanks.why: Mismatched casing that only breaks on a case-sensitive filesystem is the textbook signature of this category.

blanks.prompt: Why does it pass locally for every developer, given they're all on macOS?
blanks.why: Same mechanism as the worked example's Button/button case — macOS treats the mismatched casing as the same file, so nothing local ever exposes it.

blanks.prompt: What's the actual fix — patch the test, or something else? (a few words)
blanks.answer: fix the import's casing to match the real filename
accept: rename the import to match the file
blanks.why: The import itself is wrong; fixing it at the source (rather than adding a workaround) closes the gap for every future case-sensitive environment, not just this one CI run.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the category from the symptom's shape → narrow using the specific details → check the actual environment values → fix at the source, not by patching the symptom.** Patching a test's expected value or adding a special case for CI treats the gap as permanent instead of closing it.

contentSections.body: A CI-only failure is evidence about a real difference between two environments — read the log for which difference, then close it, rather than patching around it.

title: Flaky tests and the trust they cost
description: Why a test that's occasionally wrong for reasons unrelated to the code is more expensive than no test at all, what it actually trains a team to do, and what a real fix looks like versus what just hides the symptom.

learningObjectives.text: Analyze the actual mechanism by which flaky tests erode a team's trust in CI results
Distinguish a genuine fix for flakiness from one that masks it

contentSections.title: What a flaky test actually trains people to do

contentSections.body: A test that fails 1 run in 15, for reasons that have nothing to do with the code, doesn't cost the team those occasional few minutes of re-running. It costs something much bigger and much slower to notice: it teaches everyone what to do the next time any test goes red.

contentSections.scenario: Six months into living with a known-flaky test, a genuine regression ships to production — the same test that's 'always flaky' actually caught it, correctly, in CI, and the team re-ran the job and merged anyway.
contentSections.question: What's the real mechanism that let this happen?

options.label: The team had learned a reflex — 're-run and move on' — that applies identically to a real failure and a familiar flake, because CI can't tell them apart and neither could the team anymore
The test itself is badly written and should be deleted
Nobody was paying attention that day specifically

feedback.reflex: Right. This isn't about one distracted moment — it's a trained response built up over months of the same test crying wolf. The team's process for handling 'this test failed' had quietly become 'try again,' and that process makes no distinction between a real regression and the familiar flake, because from the outside they look identical.
feedback.bad-test: The test may well have real underlying value — it caught the actual regression correctly this time. The problem isn't that the test is worthless, it's that its flakiness taught the team to stop trusting its result either way.
feedback.inattention: Framing it as one person's bad day misses the pattern — this is a predictable, repeatable outcome of any team living with an unaddressed flaky test long enough, not a one-off lapse.

contentSections.mechanism: A test's value isn't just whether it can catch a bug — it's whether a red result actually changes what someone does. A flaky test slowly decouples those two things: it can still catch a real bug, but the team's learned response to red no longer depends on whether the bug is real. That's the actual cost, and it's invisible until the exact day it isn't.

contentSections.body: This connects directly back to the previous module's third lesson (fast, deterministic, independent) — this is what happens downstream when that property gets violated and nobody addresses it. The determinism property isn't a nice-to-have for its own sake; it's what keeps a red result meaning something specific enough that a reasonable person's response to it stays calibrated to reality instead of to "how often is this test usually right."

contentSections.scenario: A survey of engineering teams with at least one known-flaky test in their required CI checks.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of these teams report having, at some point, merged a change specifically because a real CI failure was mistaken for the known flake?
contentSections.explanation: This number varies by survey and team, but the pattern is consistently common rather than rare — a majority of teams living with an unaddressed flaky test report at least one incident of exactly this shape. The point isn't the precise figure; it's that this isn't a hypothetical edge case, it's close to the expected, typical outcome of leaving a flaky test in the required set for long enough.

contentSections.body: A flaky test's real cost isn't the false failures — it's what those failures train a team to do about every failure, including the real ones.

contentSections.title: Fixes that work versus fixes that hide it

contentSections.body: Not every response to a flaky test is equal. Some make the underlying non-determinism go away; some just make it stop showing up in the CI result, which is a very different and much worse thing.

contentSections.scenario: A test intermittently fails because it depends on `Date.now()` inside the function under test, and the assertion is time-sensitive.
contentSections.question: Which of these responses actually fixes the underlying flakiness, rather than hiding it? Select all that apply.

items.label: Mock the clock to a fixed value for the test, so the function's behavior no longer depends on real wall-clock time
Add automatic retry so a failed run gets a second chance before being reported
Widen the assertion's tolerance so small timing variance no longer causes a failure
Move the test to a separate, non-blocking suite permanently, with no plan to return to it

explanation.mock-clock: This removes the actual source of non-determinism — the test no longer depends on real time at all, so its result is now genuinely deterministic rather than merely less likely to fail.
explanation.retry: This is the auto-retry trap from the previous module — it papers over the non-determinism instead of removing it, and can let a genuinely broken test pass on lucky attempts.
explanation.widen: If the underlying behavior really does have legitimate small variance (e.g. a network-timed operation where a few milliseconds of jitter is expected and fine), widening the tolerance to match reality is a real fix — it's making the assertion accurately reflect what 'correct' means, not hiding a bug.
explanation.quarantine-silent: Moving a flaky test out of the blocking suite is sometimes the right short-term triage — but doing it permanently, with no plan to return, just relocates the same problem (a test nobody trusts) somewhere it's even easier to forget about entirely.

contentSections.synthesis: The real test: does the fix change what determines the test's outcome (mocking the clock, correcting an unrealistic tolerance) or does it just change how failures get reported (retry, permanent silent quarantine)? Only the first kind actually restores the property the test needs to be worth anything.

contentSections.body: A fix that changes what determines the test's result is a real fix. A fix that changes how failures get reported is a delay.

title: Gates worth having: what must pass before merge
description: How to decide which checks earn a blocking spot before merge — fast, deterministic, and catching something that actually matters — and why more required checks isn't automatically a safer pipeline.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a proposed CI check deserves to be a blocking gate
Distinguish a check worth blocking merge on from one worth running advisory-only

contentSections.title: The three questions a gate has to answer yes to

contentSections.body: A pipeline with 14 required checks feels thorough. Whether it's actually safer than one with 6 depends entirely on what each of those 14 checks catches — and a generated "make the pipeline more robust" pass tends to add checks for the sake of having more, not because each one earned its place.

contentSections.scenario: A team is deciding whether a new 35-minute end-to-end browser test suite, with a known 1-in-8 flake rate, should be a required blocking check on every pull request.
contentSections.question: Should it block every merge?

options.label: No — it fails the fast-and-deterministic requirement even though what it catches matters; better run on a schedule or before release
Yes — end-to-end coverage is always worth blocking on
Only on Fridays

feedback.no: Right. What it catches can be genuinely valuable — that's not in question. But a 35-minute, 1-in-8-flaky check blocking every single merge means every PR pays that cost and that flake risk, which is exactly the setup that produces the 'just re-run it' reflex from the previous lesson. Running it on a schedule, or as a required check only before a release, gets the value without making it a routine tax on every merge.
feedback.yes: Coverage mattering isn't sufficient on its own — a check has to also be fast and reliable enough that blocking on it doesn't create the exact trust-eroding pattern the previous lesson covered.
feedback.fridays: There's no principled reason tied to the day of the week — the actual criteria are about the check's own properties (speed, reliability, what it catches), not the calendar.

contentSections.concept: A blocking gate earns its place by answering yes to three separate questions: **does it catch something that would actually be expensive to ship broken**, **is it fast enough that blocking on it doesn't become a routine tax**, and **is it reliable enough that a failure means something real**. A check can matter a great deal and still fail the second or third question — which doesn't mean cutting it, it means it belongs somewhere other than blocking every merge.

contentSections.body: It's worth being explicit that this is a judgment call with real tradeoffs, not a formula — a security-critical check might be worth blocking on even at real cost to speed, because what it catches is expensive enough to justify the tax. The three questions aren't a pass/fail test, they're the actual conversation a team should be having about each required check, instead of accumulating checks by default because a generated pipeline config added them and nobody looked closely.

contentSections.question: Why might a low-stakes, fast, perfectly reliable check — like a formatting linter — still not be worth making a hard-blocking gate, even though it passes all three questions reasonably well?
contentSections.answer: Because a formatting issue is usually auto-fixable rather than needing a human decision — the better move is often to auto-format on commit or in CI and skip the human entirely, rather than blocking a person's merge over something a machine could have just silently corrected. Blocking is for things that need a human's attention; auto-fixing is for things that don't.
contentSections.hint: Is blocking-and-asking-a-human the only response available for a check like this, or is there a cheaper one?

contentSections.body: A gate belongs in the blocking set only if it catches something expensive, runs fast, and is reliable enough that its result means something.

contentSections.title: Pruning a pipeline that's grown by default

contentSections.body: A generated CI config, asked to "be thorough," tends to add checks rather than question them — nothing about generating a config from a prompt naturally prunes what doesn't earn its keep. That's a human judgment call, every time.

contentSections.scenario: A pipeline has 14 required checks. You're reviewing which ones genuinely deserve to block merge.
contentSections.question: Which of these are the right questions to ask about each check, to decide if it should stay blocking? Select all that apply.

items.label: What has this check actually caught in the last few months — real bugs, or nothing?
How many total checks does the pipeline currently have?
How long does it take, and does that cost get paid on every single merge?
How often does it fail for reasons unrelated to the actual change being merged?

explanation.catches: The most direct evidence: a check with months of history and zero real catches is a strong candidate to demote, regardless of how reasonable it sounded when it was added.
explanation.count: The total count of checks isn't itself informative — a pipeline with 20 well-chosen checks can be better than one with 6 badly-chosen ones. Each check is evaluated on its own, not against a target number.
explanation.speed: Directly determines whether the check is a routine tax on every merge or a rare, tolerable cost.
explanation.reliable: Directly determines whether a failure means something real often enough to justify blocking on it.

contentSections.synthesis: None of the right questions are about the pipeline's total size — a bloated-feeling pipeline isn't fixed by picking an arbitrary number to cut down to, it's fixed by evaluating each check against what it actually catches, how fast it is, and how reliable it is, and demoting or removing the ones that don't earn their blocking status on those merits.

contentSections.body: A pipeline gets safer by evaluating what each check actually catches, not by having more checks or fewer — size was never the real variable.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose CI-only failures from log evidence alone, at speed

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Same diagnostic habits as the lessons, eight fresh failures to read. One sitting or several — nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for on the checkpoint.

title: Lab — Make a Generated Project Build the Same Way Twice
description: Take a generated project whose build only reliably works on the machine that generated it, and turn it into one that builds clean from a genuinely fresh checkout — with a record of exactly what you had to fix to get there.

learningObjectives.text: Identify undeclared environment assumptions in a real generated project
Convert those assumptions into declared, pinned, reproducible requirements

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the module's real test: not spotting a reproducibility gap in an example, but hunting one down and closing it in something you're actually looking at.

contentSections.title: Make a generated project build the same way twice
contentSections.brief: You've been handed a project (recently generated, or use one of your own that was AI-assisted) that its author says "works fine" on their machine. Your job is to find every place its build depends on something undeclared, and fix it — proving, not assuming, that it now builds cleanly from a genuinely fresh environment.
contentSections.deliverable: A project that builds clean from a fresh checkout, plus a short list of every undeclared assumption you found and what you changed to close each one.

stages.title: Audit the setup instructions line by line
stages.instructions: Read the project's README or setup instructions as a stranger with a bare machine would. For every command, ask: does this assume a tool, a runtime version, an environment variable, or a system library that isn't declared anywhere in the project itself? List each undeclared assumption you find.
stages.checkpoint: You have a list of specific undeclared assumptions, each naming the exact tool/version/variable, not a vague 'setup might be incomplete.'

stages.title: Check whether dependencies are actually pinned
stages.instructions: Check whether a lockfile exists and is committed, whether the CI (or deploy) process uses a strict, lockfile-respecting install command, and whether the runtime version (language/framework) is pinned to a specific version rather than 'latest' or unspecified.
stages.checkpoint: You can state, for each of the three (lockfile committed, install command strict, runtime pinned), whether it's currently true or false.

stages.title: Fix every gap and prove it with a fresh build
stages.instructions: For each gap found in stages 1 and 2, make the fix: declare the missing tool/dependency explicitly, commit and enforce the lockfile, pin the runtime version. Then actually attempt a build from a genuinely fresh environment — a clean container, a fresh clone in a new directory with a cleared cache, or the closest equivalent you have access to — and record whether it succeeds without any manual intervention beyond the declared, documented steps.
stages.checkpoint: Every gap from stages 1 and 2 has a corresponding fix, and you have a specific record of the fresh-environment build attempt: what happened, and if it failed, what the remaining gap was and how you closed it.

rubric.criterion: Undeclared assumptions were found by actually auditing, not guessed at
rubric.meets: Each item in the list names a specific command and what it silently assumes, traceable to a real line in the setup instructions or build config.

rubric.criterion: Pinning was checked for all three: lockfile, strict install, runtime version
rubric.meets: All three have an explicit true/false stated, with evidence (a file, a config line) rather than an assumption.

rubric.criterion: Every found gap has a real fix, not a workaround
rubric.meets: Fixes declare the requirement explicitly (in a manifest, Dockerfile, or CI config) rather than papering over the symptom — matching lesson three's 'fix at the source' standard.

rubric.criterion: The fresh build was actually attempted, not assumed
rubric.meets: There's a specific record of a real fresh-environment build attempt and its outcome, not a claim that the fixes 'should' work.

rubric.criterion: The deliverable is legible to a teammate
rubric.meets: A teammate could read the list of fixes and understand exactly what was undeclared before and what changed, without re-deriving your investigation.

contentSections.body: A build that's provably reproducible from a fresh environment is a different, stronger claim than a build that's merely worked so far — now you have the evidence for which one you actually have.

title: Checkpoint — CI, Builds and Reproducibility
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Review Workflow and PR Craft, two pulling further back to Tests You Can Trust. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — CI, Builds and Reproducibility

questions.from: This module — It works here: the environment you forgot you had
questions.prompt: Why does a build 'working' on the author's machine not guarantee it works elsewhere?

options.label: It may silently depend on tools or versions installed on that machine for unrelated reasons, never declared in the project
Every machine runs code identically once the source is the same
It only matters if the author has a slow computer

questions.explanation: A machine's accumulated global installs are invisible to the project unless explicitly declared — CI's clean environment is what exposes this gap.

questions.from: This module — Lockfiles, pinned versions, and reproducible installs
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between a version range like ^2.1.0 and a lockfile entry?

options.label: The range describes what's allowed to install; the lockfile records what actually did
They mean exactly the same thing
Lockfiles are only relevant for Python projects

questions.explanation: A range permits movement within it on every fresh install; a lockfile pins the exact resolved version tree from a real install.

questions.from: This module — Reading a CI failure that didn't happen locally
questions.prompt: A `Module not found` error on Linux CI, never seen locally on macOS, most likely points to what?

options.label: Case sensitivity — macOS forgives mismatched import casing, Linux doesn't
A CI provider outage
A syntax error only Linux can detect

questions.explanation: This is one of the most common CI-only failure signatures — a filesystem case mismatch that a case-insensitive local filesystem silently forgives.

questions.from: This module — Flaky tests and the trust they cost
questions.prompt: What's the real long-term cost of an unaddressed flaky test in required CI checks?

options.label: It trains the team to treat red as ambiguous, so real failures get dismissed the same way as the familiar flake
It slightly increases CI compute costs and nothing else
It has no real cost as long as it's rare

questions.explanation: The cost isn't the false failures themselves — it's the learned response to every red build afterward, including genuine ones.

questions.from: Previous module — Splitting a large generated change into reviewable pieces
questions.prompt: Why split a large generated change by dependency order rather than by file type?

options.label: So each piece is independently verifiable against something real, not a stub
It produces fewer total pull requests
It matches most linters' default configuration

questions.explanation: Dependency order lets each piece be tested and reviewed against real, already-merged pieces rather than requiring the whole feature to judge any one part.

questions.from: Previous module — Disclosing what was generated, and why it matters to the reviewer
questions.prompt: What makes a disclosure statement actually useful to a reviewer?

options.label: It names what was generated, what was checked, and where confidence is lowest
It states that AI was involved somewhere
It includes an apology for using AI assistance

questions.explanation: A generic 'AI-assisted' carries almost no information anymore — the useful version routes the reviewer's attention to a specific place.

questions.from: Previous module — Responding to review on code you didn't write
questions.prompt: A reviewer questions a decision in generated code you can't currently explain. What's the accountable response?

options.label: Say you don't know, then find out whether the decision is load-bearing or arbitrary, and report back
Say 'the AI generated it that way' and move on
Defend it confidently to keep the review moving

questions.explanation: 'The AI wrote it' describes provenance, not correctness — the reviewer asked about correctness, which requires actually finding out.

questions.from: Previous module — The pull request description as the reviewer's only context
questions.prompt: What does a cold reviewer know that only the PR description can tell them?

options.label: Everything the author knows that isn't visible in the diff itself — why, what's tested, what to focus on
The exact line count of the change
Nothing — the diff alone is always sufficient

questions.explanation: The description is the interface for everything the author knows that the diff can't show on its own.

questions.from: Two modules back — A test is a claim about behaviour someone will rely on
questions.prompt: What makes a test a claim someone can rely on, rather than decoration?

options.label: It asserts a specific expected outcome that would change if the code were wrong
It runs quickly as part of CI
It has a descriptive name

questions.explanation: A fast, well-named test that only checks 'didn't throw' still can't distinguish correct behaviour from most kinds of wrong behaviour.

questions.from: Two modules back — Fast, deterministic, and independent — or nobody runs them
questions.prompt: A test hits a real third-party API and occasionally fails when that API is slow. Which property does this violate?

options.label: Determinism — the outcome now depends on something other than the code
Independence — it depends on another test's leftover state
Nothing, as long as it usually passes

questions.explanation: The test's result now depends on the third party's uptime and latency, not on whether the code is correct.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back today returns in a later checkpoint — that's the design.
